Our Bayesian strategy provides uncertainty quantification for the inferred density ratio, which is critical for applications involving high-dimensional and data-limited distributions with potentially substantial uncertainty. We further show connections of the balancing loss to the exponential loss in binary classification and to the variational form of f-divergence, particularly the squared Hellinger distance. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed boosting algorithms achieve high accuracy at low computational cost, and that the Bayesian additive tree is competitive in accuracy while additionally providing uncertainty quantification, which the compared estimators do not offer. Finally, we demonstrate its application to assessing the quality of generative models for microbiome compositional data.

items.title: LLM knowledge for improved Out-of-Distribution Tabular Prediction - A Cross-Validated Regularisation Approach
items.summary: Prediction models degrade when the deployment population differs from the one used to train them, and training data cannot say which feature-response relationships will transfer. Expert elicitation is slow and unscalable. We ask whether coefficient priors elicited from large language models (LLMs) improve out-of-distribution (OOD) prediction as the shrinkage target of a regularised regression instead of zero, across five tabular datasets split on real covariates, selecting providers and prior structures by source-domain cross-validation alone. The priors help on four of five datasets, by up to 7.9% OOD mean squared error, and ten of twenty-four prior-informed results resolve the mean improvement at conventional confidence; single-deployment intervals are much wider. On classification the gain is in probabilistic accuracy, not ranking, and control tests with corrupted priors attribute the benefit to feature-specific content rather than scale. Two findings temper this. Variation across candidate priors exceeds the average benefit, yet cross-validation margins fall below their own noise, so selection avoids the worst prior rather than finding the best. On three datasets the prior improves in-domain accuracy as much as out-of-domain, making it better regularisation than shift correction. Only where the training data are large enough that the in-domain gain disappears does elicited knowledge demonstrably improve transfer. Code, priors and results: https://github.com/hugohammer/llm-priors-ood.

items.title: Bayesian Treed Vecchia Gaussian Process Emulation via Sequential Monte Carlo
items.summary: Computer models (or simulators) are used in many scientific domains to understand and predict real-world processes, but they are expensive to run. One way to address this hurdle is to use Gaussian processes (GPs). For complex physical systems such as storm surge, simulator outputs often exhibit heterogeneous structures, and many nonstationary GP methods become impractical with several inputs and tens of thousands of runs. To address these issues, we combine the divide-and-conquer idea of treed GP models with Vecchia approximations in a Bayesian treed Vecchia GP (TVGP) model. The model uses the Bayesian classification and regression tree prior for random recursive partitioning of the input domain. Within each leaf, a Vecchia approximation allows efficient likelihood evaluation. For Bayesian inference, we develop a sequential Monte Carlo algorithm that explores tree space as an alternative to reversible-jump Markov chain Monte Carlo. The method is demonstrated on synthetic examples with two and ten inputs and on a storm-surge simulator with seven inputs and up to 50,649 training runs. TVGP has the smallest prediction error in both synthetic examples and with the larger storm-surge training set, although its predictive intervals undercover in the example with ten inputs and the storm-surge application.

items.title: Hilbert-Scale Stability of Posterior Diffusion Priors for Ill-Posed Signal Recovery
items.summary: Indirect and noisy observations are difficult to invert when the forward operator smooths out the unknown signal. In this case, the unstable modes are precisely the modes that the data reveals least, thus the success of any reconstruction method depends on how prior information interacts with the geometry of the operator across regularity scales. Diffusion priors have become ubiquitous for such problems; however, the current theory still does not determine when a learned score remains informative under ill-posed forward operators. In this paper, we study posterior diffusion for linear inverse problems on Hilbert scales and derive a stability theory under an explicit score-amplification condition. Under a smoothing condition on the forward map, a source condition on the truth, and weak-norm control of score error, we derive non-asymptotic recovery bounds in \(\Hs^s\) that separate observation noise, score approximation, and reverse-time discretization. These bounds give a recoverable regularity threshold determined jointly by operator smoothing, truth regularity, score regularity, and the posterior correction. The threshold specifies the Hilbert-scale norms \(\Hs^s\) in which weak-norm score error remains controlled after propagation through the posterior reverse dynamics. For larger regularity indices \(s\), the inverse geometry magnifies the same error, and the Hilbert-scale recovery estimate no longer gives uniform stability. We also prove that a posterior correction adapted to the forward operator improves stability relative to isotropic guidance in the regularity ranges where the smoothing action of the forward map matters most. The recovery estimates give a regularity-sensitive theory of posterior diffusion and show how learned score error, operator smoothing, and reconstruction norm jointly determine the stable range predicted by the analysis.

items.title: Generative Refinement Learning for Temporal Interpolation in Scientific Machine Learning
items.summary: Computationally expensive simulations and real-world observations often provide data at a lower temporal resolution than downstream tasks require. Averaging observations at fixed grid points can introduce errors, and motion estimates alone do not determine how the physical field values change. In this work, we study whether learning to correct a simple numerical interpolation improves the reconstruction of intermediate scientific fields. Our model, interpolative FLow EXpert (iFLEX), first estimates the missing field by taking a weighted average of the two observations at each grid point, giving more weight to the observation closer to the requested time. During training, subtracting this estimate from an observed intermediate field gives the residual that a conditional diffusion model learns to generate. Both observations condition the model, together with the target time, the interval between observations, and available physical parameters. To reconstruct an unobserved intermediate field, the generated residual is added to the weighted average. We evaluate iFLEX on Navier-Stokes Kraichnan turbulence, Shanghai radar precipitation, and sea surface temperature. Across these datasets, iFLEX achieves lower reconstruction error than the evaluated baselines, including optical-flow and diffusion models developed for video frame interpolation in computer vision. In a controlled turbulence comparison at a Reynolds number of 36,000, learning the residual reduces relative Frobenius norm error from about 13.7 for direct field generation to 10.5, with the diffusion backbone and training setup held fixed. Code is available at https://github.com/paulpuren/iflex.

items.title: Momentum in large-batch training: Polyak enlarges the critical batch size, Nesterov improves data efficiency
items.summary: We study when and how momentum improves large-batch training in the one-pass regime, using power-law kernel regression as a tractable setting. We first characterize stochastic stability through the \emph{critical learning rate}, defined as the largest learning rate for stable training, and obtain $η_{\mathrm{SGD}}^{\mathrm{crit}}\eqsim 1$, $η_{\mathrm{Polyak}}^{\mathrm{crit}}\eqsim \min\{1,B(1-β)\}$, and $η_{\mathrm{Nesterov}}^{\mathrm{crit}}\eqsim \min\{1,B^q(1-β)\}$, where $B$ is the batch size, $β\in[0,1)$ is the momentum factor, and \(q>1\) is the capacity exponent governing spectral decay. Within the stable region, we derive scaling laws for the full risk dynamics, capturing the progression from an early transient through power-law decay to a noise floor. We then optimize the final-step risk under a fixed data budget, obtaining a three-regime phase diagram that reveals how the benefits of momentum change with batch size. Notably, Polyak enlarges the critical batch size, the largest batch size preserving the optimal small-batch data-scaling exponent, thereby allowing fewer sequential updates without sacrificing data efficiency. In contrast, Nesterov improves the optimal data-scaling exponent in the large-batch regime through look-ahead-induced suppression of noise amplification. Experiments on PLK regression quantitatively support the theoretical scaling predictions, while neural-network experiments provide qualitative evidence for the predicted batch-size dependence and stability behavior.

items.title: Conservative Dueling Bandits: Preference Learning under Baseline Constraints
items.summary: Contextual dueling bandits learn from pairwise comparisons, the same feedback used to fine-tune language models from human preferences. Standard algorithms explore aggressively and can show users two poor options. We study conservative contextual dueling bandits, which require that, at every round, the cumulative score of the better displayed item stay above a $(1-α)$ fraction of a trusted baseline's. An item's score is its probability of beating the best available item, so the constraint depends only on utility differences and needs no absolute rewards. This also changes how safety can be certified: we show that transferring the safety test of the conservative bandit algorithm CLUCB unchanged can incur linear regret, even when the baseline's utilities are known exactly. For linear utilities, we develop MaxInP-BC, which certifies scores through utility gaps and, when it must fall back, pairs the baseline with an informative partner so that fallback rounds still drive learning. It is safe with high probability at all times, with regret $\tilde{O}(d\sqrt{T}/κ)$ plus an additive cost of conservatism that does not grow with the horizon. For general utility classes, we develop BTIGW-BC, which turns the guarantee of an online logistic-regression oracle into cumulative safety certificates. It is safe at all times, makes finitely many fallbacks, and has sublinear regret whenever the oracle's logistic regret is sublinear. In experiments, both satisfy the constraint, which their unconstrained counterparts often violate, at a moderate cost in regret.

items.title: Bias-Aware Guardrail Selection Under Network Interference
items.summary: Web platforms use randomized experiment logs to choose budget-feasible treatment allocations while limiting losses to a designated group of units. Under network interference, each allocation requires expected outcomes at treatment-exposure pairs that may be sparsely observed. Existing safe policy selection methods require valid inference for each candidate, but pooling nearby exposures to improve estimability can introduce allocation-specific bias that variance-only bounds omit. We propose exposure-stratified guardrail selection (ESGuard), which aggregates unit-level bias bounds into a bias bound on each candidate's guardrail effect. It incorporates these bounds into simultaneous lower confidence bounds to select an allocation or retain the status quo. Under randomized rounds, a correct exposure mapping, and valid curvature and slope bounds, the conditional bias bound holds in finite samples. With independent rounds and additional regularity conditions, the unconditional probability of selecting an unsafe allocation is asymptotically at most the target level. We evaluate ESGuard on a simulator built from New York City ride-hailing trips. With six months of simulated rounds, we compare estimators that pool nearby exposures on the same logs and candidate sets. Adding the bias bound raises simultaneous coverage from below the nominal 95 percent level to at least 95 percent for every estimator in this comparison. In the underserved-only scenario, ESGuard violates the guardrail in 0.06 percent of its selections, compared with 16 percent for the point-estimate rule under the same gain ranking, and abstains in about a quarter of replications. Omitted spillovers can invalidate the protection. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/esguard-4D2E/.

items.title: Robust Log-Contrast Regression for High-Dimensional Compositional Microbiome Data with Outliers
items.summary: It is well known that microbiome sequencing data are naturally compositional and often have a complex subcomposition structure, as well as a lot of noise and some outliers. These characteristics make classical log-contrast regression difficult to apply, because it is sensitive to extreme values and cannot fully meet the linear constraints of compositional predictors. To tackle these issues, in this paper, we propose a robust log-contrast regression framework that incorporates the Huber loss function along with a Lasso penalty, which not only boosts resistance to outliers but also facilitates sparse variable selection. It is important to note that the general linear constraints, which are explicitly imposed, serve to preserve the algebraic coherence of compositional and subcompositional covariates. Under some mild assumptions, we theoretically prove that the proposed method achieves non-asymptotic guarantees in finite samples, comparable to those of Huber loss estimators, ensuring robustness. To implement the method efficiently, we develop a symmetric Gauss--Seidel-based alternating direction method of multipliers based on its dual formulation with a convergence guarantee, and it is also easy to implement in the sense that each subproblem admits a closed-form solution. To evaluate the statistical performance of the proposed method, we conduct a series of numerical experiments using simulated data and gut microbiome data, which show that the proposed method achieves better estimation accuracy, competitive prediction performance, and more reliable outlier identification than the benchmark method RobRegCC.

items.title: Kähler landscapes for complex neural network descents and guarantees including a search and destroy of the Calabi-Yau manifold
items.summary: We study landscapes for complex-parameterized networks. Our approach is motivated with an information-theoretic manifold perspective of the parameter and via classical optimization guarantees although of complex geometric variety such as through Dolbeault asymptotics. The descent path admits a Kähler information metric under a cross-entropy via the Wirtinger Hessian on the log-likelihood potential. We restrict attention to a descent update rule with natural gradient descent via a differentiated loss scaled by the inverse metric, so the descent path remains in the holomorphic tangent bundle. We emphasize Calabi-Yau information manifolds which profane theoretical guarantees via an ill-curvature-conditioned, or lack thereof, landscape. We focus on Calabi-Yau metrics specifically in a non-compact setting with a global potential, so defined geometrically rather than invoking the topological requirements of the Calabi conjecture. In non-compact settings, we can write the metric determinant with respect to a background in terms of a function, pluriharmonic or real. Using Yau's Liouville theorem, we get a partial eigenvalue blow-up effect. In an empirical setting, a Ricci-flat metric will not form, but a blow-up can be a local condition and can hold empirically on open sets even partially in generalized Kähler cases due to lower bounds on the Ricci potential. Moreover, it has been discovered that negative curvature subverts the loss landscape, specifically sectional curvature, so we expand on this and draw interconnections to negative-definite Ricci curvature. Our arguments primarily exist via geometric modality, although we establish roots in deep learning theory such as through asymptotics at initialization and connections through failure modes of neural network guarantees under vanishing and negative Ricci curvature.

items.title: Coupled unbiased MCMC for estimating Shapley effects under dependent inputs
items.summary: In global sensitivity analysis, Shapley effects provide a game-theoretic allocation of output variance among potentially dependent inputs. Their computation typically requires repeated conditional sampling, which can be challenging even when independent samples from the joint input distribution can be generated exactly. This difficulty arises naturally in hierarchical models, where conditioning on arbitrary subsets need not follow the generative order. To efficiently estimate Shapley effects under such dependence between input variables, we propose a permutation-based framework using coupled unbiased Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC). Our proposed method combines two complementary coupling mechanisms: (i) a joint coupling of conditional distributions along a random permutation, designed to reduce the variance of estimated marginal contributions, and (ii) a meeting-based coupling of Markov chains that removes finite-time MCMC bias through a telescoping correction. Under suitable conditions, we prove that the resulting estimators for the unnormalized Shapley effects are unbiased, and have finite variance and finite expected computational cost. Numerical experiments with various test cases illustrate the computational efficiency of the proposed method.

items.title: An Asymptotic Theory of Chain-of-Thought in In-Context Learning
items.summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning has become a widely used mechanism for eliciting multi-step reasoning in large language models by generating intermediate reasoning steps at inference time. Yet the scaling behavior of generalization with CoT depth remains poorly understood. To address this question, we study a theoretically solvable model of CoT for in-context weight prediction in linear regression, where test-time reasoning is represented as an iterative refinement of the weight-parameter estimate. Using tools from random matrix theory under high-dimensional asymptotics, we derive an exact formula for the generalization error as a function of reasoning depth, pretraining data amount, and context length. Our analysis reveals a sharp phase transition separating exponential and polynomial improvement, saturation, and overthinking, and characterizes how the optimal reasoning depth scales. We further show that deeper reasoning is most effective with sufficiently rich pretraining and in-context information, whereas limited pretraining or context makes longer reasoning prone to error amplification or saturation. We also validate these predictions through experiments on fully learned linear attention and softmax attention models. Our results provide a unified theoretical account of how test-time CoT depth affects generalization.

items.title: PDE-Based Bounds on Optimal Exponents in Active Simple Hypothesis Testing
items.summary: We present general upper and lower bounds on the optimal error exponent for the Active Simple Hypothesis Testing (ASHT) problem. ASHT has been extensively studied across diverse fields including Information Theory, Bandits, and Operations Research, a precise characterization of this optimal exponent has remained elusive. This work combines a recent Partial Differential Equation (PDE) characterization of the optimal exponent by Vijayan (2025) with the comparison principle of viscosity solutions of Hamilton-Jacobi PDEs. This leads to bounds that are parametrized by convex functions, sets and lower Hamiltonian relaxations, a flexibility that generalizes many known results in the literature.

items.title: Deep Bayesian Approaches for Interpretable Nonlinear Structural System Identification
items.summary: System identification, namely the inference of mathematical representations of dynamical systems from measured data, is fundamental to engineering diagnostics, prognostics, and decision-making. Bayesian filtering offers a principled framework for probabilistic state estimation but traditionally relies on prescribed transition and observation models. Recent advances in deep Bayesian filtering address this limitation by embedding learnable representations within probabilistic state-space formulations, enabling data-driven identification of unknown dynamics while retaining physical structure and uncertainty-aware inference. This tutorial provides a systematic introduction to deep Bayesian filtering for nonlinear structural system identification, focusing on the interplay between learned dynamics, physical inductive biases, and posterior inference. The Deep Markov Model serves as a data-driven reference, while the Physics-guided Deep Markov Model (PgDMM) and Neural Extended Kalman Filter (Neural EKF) illustrate complementary approaches based on amortized variational inference and differentiable Kalman filtering, respectively. Their capabilities are examined through dynamic state estimation and joint dynamic state and parameter estimation on a three-dimensional shear-frame benchmark with hysteretic Bouc-Wen connections and sparse acceleration measurements. The results highlight important distinctions between measurement-conditioned reconstruction and open-loop forecasting, demonstrate how physical structure can improve latent-state interpretability without necessarily ensuring predictive fidelity, and reveal differences in the robustness of response and parameter estimation. Practical guidelines for model construction, training, evaluation, and deployment are provided, together with an outlook on remaining challenges in uncertainty calibration, identifiability, and real-world validation.

items.title: The uneven rise of AI-generated web content
items.summary: In less than five years, generative artificial intelligence (AI) has dramatically reshaped the public-facing web. Using a sample of more than 5 million crawlable webpages, we demonstrate that the share containing AI-generated text has increased precipitously, but unevenly. Our analyses reveal substantial differences in AI composition across language and domain categories (e.g., .edu, .com, or .gov). A higher fraction of English-language webpages contain AI-generated text compared to pages in other languages, and prevalence is substantially lower on .gov and .edu domains compared to .com. These distinctions persist even after accounting for compositional effects. We also find heterogeneity based on a page's position in the connectivity structure of the web. AI-generated text is most common and has increased most rapidly in pages that are the least central in the graph, which drives much of the overall growth in AI-generated text. A slower increase has taken place for more central pages, with the most central tier emerging as the least likely to contain AI-generated text. Methodologically, we use multiple AI detection tools, and generate estimates using a Bayesian hierarchical model that incorporates corrections for the detectors' statistical properties (both false positives and false negatives) and allows for different detector performance across groups, while propagating uncertainty in detector error rates into prevalence estimates. Our work suggests that AI is a prominent, but varied, contributor to public information and internet-based communication.

items.title: Modeling Dependence Structures in Astronomical Multi-Band Time Series Data via Multi-Output Gaussian Processes
items.summary: Modern astronomical time-domain surveys routinely collect multi-band light curves that provide complementary information about the physical processes governing source variability. Although various multi-output Gaussian process (GP) models have been applied in different astronomical contexts, the statistical and astrophysical implications of their dependence structures have received comparatively limited attention. In this work, we examine three existing approaches to modeling cross-band dependence within a common multi-output GP framework and investigate how their underlying assumptions affect statistical inference and astrophysical interpretation. These include covariance-based, stochastic differential equation (SDE)-based, and latent-process approaches, which differ mainly in how cross-band dependence is introduced. The covariance-based approach directly specifies cross-band covariance functions to characterize dependence, whereas the SDE-based approach specifies joint temporal dynamics, with cross-band dependence arising from coupled dynamics or correlated driving processes. The latent-process approach represents dependence through shared stochastic processes and their transformations, which can reflect physical relationships among multiple light curves. We demonstrate the practical implications of these modeling choices through applications to multi-band active galactic nucleus light curves and emission-line reverberation mapping. Rather than advocating a universally preferred approach, this work provides guidance for selecting dependence structures according to scientific objectives and clarifies how these choices influence the statistical characterization and scientific interpretation of multi-band stochastic variability.

items.title: Balanced State Subspaces for Mamba-2 State Compression
items.summary: Mamba-2 compresses all context into a fixed-size recurrent state that dominates decoding memory and bandwidth. Existing compressors quantize state values or prune state coordinates, scoring each channel independently in the native basis. We examine trained Mamba-2 states and find that energy is almost rank-one, but the output does not read the energetic directions: energy concentrates in a bias-like direction accumulated by the recurrence, while the content the output reads lives in a low-dimensional subspace that is not aligned with the state's coordinates. Even output-aware scores are computed coordinate by coordinate, so they miss the directions that determine the input--output map. Compression should therefore target the write--read subspace rather than individual coordinates. We propose \method{}, a post-training transform that instantiates balanced truncation with full controllability and observability Gramians and applies the rotation exactly via Mamba-2's scalar-identity transition. Because the useful rank varies widely across layers, we further introduce HARP, which allocates ranks per layer from the Hankel spectrum and protects retrieval-sensitive layers, improving both perplexity and retrieval over uniform budgets. Calibration takes a single forward pass, an order of magnitude faster than GHOST's released protocol, with lower peak memory. With HARP, \method{} halves the state dimension at an average WikiText-2 perplexity increase of $0.3$ points ($1.8\%$) across 130M--2.7B, versus $1.6$ ($9.3\%$) for GHOST, and the gap widens at 25\% retention.

items.title: When Scatter Plots Hide the Data: Diagnosing Ties and Choosing the Right Display in R
items.summary: Scatter plots draw one mark per observation, so observations that share a location are hidden. In a two-item Likert survey of 2,757 respondents, 98.7% of the data lie under other points and the plot shows only 36 dots. The density-distribution sunflower plot of Dupont and Plummer addresses this by drawing raw points in sparse regions and sunflowers, whose petals count observations, in dense ones. It is not available in R, and its single petal weight for dense cells fails when cell counts span more than an order of magnitude: small dense cells collapse to one petal, and the count a reader decodes can be wrong by 150% or more. We propose geometric petal tiers, in which each cell uses the smallest weight among 1, b, b2, . . . observations per petal that keeps its flower within P petals. Every flower then has between about P/b and P petals, and the relative error of every decoded count is below b/(2P), 17.9% at the defaults b = 5 and P = 14. We also define tie diagnostics and decision rules that use them to choose between an ordinary scatter plot, jitter or transparency, a classic sunflower plot and geometric tiers. Both are implemented in the ggplot2 extension ggsunflower. We illustrate the methods on survey, automotive, historical and large commercial data, and in a simulation over 35 conditions geometric tiers keep the worst-cell error at or below 14% where a single weight reaches a median of 251%.

items.title: Wasserstein approximation of measures via orthogonal frames: statistical and computational complexities
items.summary: Dimension-reduction methods such as PCA identify a subspace capturing most of the variation in the data, but not a distinguished basis within it. Selecting a basis in which the samples are sparsely represented is a recurring task in unsupervised learning, addressed by methods in factor analysis, dictionary learning, and subspace clustering. We pose this task as Wasserstein approximation of the data distribution by measures supported on the axes of an orthogonal frame, which, in turn, reduces to a nonsmooth optimization problem over the orthogonal group $\mathrm{O}(d)$. We show that, under mild assumptions, both empirical risk minimizers and a locally initialized stochastic gradient method recover the population-optimal frame at the near-parametric rate $\widetilde{O}_d(n^{-1/2})$, where $n$ is the sample size. The main difficulty is that, although the population objective is smooth, the empirical objective is not-this mismatch precludes standard covering arguments. We overcome this issue by replacing Lipschitz continuity of the empirical gradient with a coarsely Lipschitz bound, a tool that may be of independent interest. Numerical experiments support our theoretical findings.

items.title: Principal Decomposition with Nested Submanifolds
items.summary: Over the past decades, the increasing dimensionality of data has increased the need for effective data decomposition methods. Existing approaches, however, often rely on linear models or lack sufficient interpretability or flexibility. To address this issue, we introduce a novel nonlinear decomposition technique called the principal nested submanifolds, which builds on the foundational concepts of principal component analysis. This method exploits the local geometric information of data sets by projecting samples onto a series of nested principal submanifolds with progressively decreasing dimensions. It effectively isolates complex information within the data in a backward stepwise manner by targeting variations associated with smaller eigenvalues in local covariance matrices. The fitted structures are smooth nested manifolds rather than linear or special-shape subspaces. Simulation studies and an analysis of single-cell RNA-sequencing data illustrate how the method summarizes locally varying nonlinear structure while retaining a compatible hierarchy across dimensions. It provides flexible subspace constraints that facilitate the extraction of data components and noise reduction. This approach advances the non-Euclidean statistical analysis of data with low-dimensional intrinsic structure within Euclidean spaces and offers a complementary perspective for high-dimensional noisy data sets in fields such as bioinformatics and machine learning.

items.title: Flexible Estimation of Covariate-Specific Win Ratio for Prioritized Time-to-Event Outcomes
items.summary: Prioritized time-to-event outcomes arise frequently in clinical studies, where treatment comparisons may be based on a prespecified hierarchy of clinically important outcomes. The win ratio provides a natural summary of treatment benefit for such prioritized outcomes. However, methods for characterizing heterogeneous treatment effects by estimating how the win ratio varies with baseline covariates remain limited in this setting. We develop a flexible local inverse probability of censoring weighted estimator of the win ratio as a function of baseline covariates, without imposing the parametric shape or proportional win-fractions structure assumed by existing regression approaches. We use best linear projections to summarize the estimated log win ratio and develop formal tests of log-linearity of the win ratio function. We also propose a complementary model-based estimator of the covariate-specific win ratio assuming proportional hazards models for the marginal distributions, copula dependence between the margins, and Bernstein-polynomial sieves for the baseline hazards. Large-sample properties and bootstrap validity are established for both approaches. Simulations show that the local estimator is robust, while the model-based procedure can provide substantial efficiency and power gains under correct specification, and proportional win-fractions regression may lead to bias when its structural assumptions fail. The methods are illustrated by analyzing data from CALGB 9633, a randomized lung cancer trial.

items.title: Nuclear Norm-Regularized Bayesian Matrix Completion
items.summary: Nuclear-norm-regularized least squares is a standard approach to matrix completion, but it yields only a point estimate. Its Bayesian counterpart, a prior combining the nuclear norm with a Frobenius-norm term, gives a strongly log-concave though nonsmooth posterior when the noise precision is known. In practice the precision is unknown, and placing a truncated Jeffreys prior on it makes the joint posterior neither log-concave nor smooth. To our knowledge, we give the first sampler for this model with an explicit non-asymptotic guarantee: its output is within a prescribed total-variation or Wasserstein distance of the posterior on the matrix after a number of steps polynomial in the matrix dimensions and the reciprocal of the target accuracy. The sampler never targets a continuous distribution that is not strongly log-concave. It discretizes the precision onto a grid, estimates its posterior by thermodynamic integration along the tilted conditional posteriors of the matrix, and bounds the error this propagates to the posterior on the matrix. The approach applies whenever non-log-concavity is confined to a bounded scalar hyperparameter and the conditional distributions are strongly log-concave with smooth-plus-Lipschitz potentials. Our result establishes feasibility; the polynomial complexity is not intended as a practical algorithm at current problem scales.

items.title: Effect-Size Estimation and Confounding-Aware Permutations for PERMANOVA
items.summary: Motivation: PERMANOVA is widely used to test associations between covariates and high-dimensional data with arbitrary distributions, such as ecology, metabolomics, or microbial community profiling. In these contexts, its effect size measure (R2) is generally used to indicate how much the high-dimensional measurement covaries with respect to a separate, univariate measure. However, as we show, this conventional effect size is inflated under the null, resulting in values that do not accurately reflect the conventional expectation of "variance explained." Furthermore, standard permutation schemes yield inflated false positives in the presence of non-independent samples, such as repeated measure designs. Results: We introduce confounding-aware permutation schemes for both invariant and variant covariates. We additionally develop a causally-grounded, distance-based effect-size estimator derived from the Hájek average treatment effect estimator, providing interpretable effect sizes in the units of the chosen dissimilarity metric. Simulations using microbiome profiles demonstrate that these approaches control false positives while maintaining power, outperforming standard PERMANOVA implementations. Availability and Implementation: An R implementation is freely available in the permaBrioche module of the bioBakery ecosystem https://huttenhower.sph.harvard.edu/permabrioche. Contact: chuttenh@hsph.harvard.edu

items.title: BRIDGE: An Acceptance Gate to Block False Improvements in Model Updates, with a Retrospective Clinical Evaluation
items.summary: Models are updated repeatedly, and an update that looks better on validation data but not on new data is a false improvement that can misguide clinical decisions. The naive rule accepts every positive validation gain and is optimistic when the same data choose and judge the update. BRIDGE is a model-agnostic acceptance gate that decides each update from predictions and the available labels, with fixed settings. Each fold of the data judges the update chosen on the other folds (cross-fitting) to reduce selection bias; acceptance requires the gain's lower bootstrap bound to exceed a margin. The four settings are (A) 11 new datasets, (B) synthetic tasks, (C) 12 retrospective clinical tasks, and (D) 39 supporting datasets. The false-improvement rate falls from 19.1% (naive) to 1.1% (BRIDGE) in (A), 20.7% to 1.7% (B), 20.0% to 0% (C), and 12.5% to 0.5% (D); every 95% confidence interval of the reduction over datasets or tasks excludes zero (not over the clinical sources). An equal-size random draw from the naive acceptances contains more false improvements in (A)-(E) (post hoc, p<0.001). On the OpenML collection (E) of 14 new datasets, the false-improvement rate falls from 25.6% to 1.0%. BRIDGE removes 97% to 100% of the false improvements that the naive rule accepts, and its mean gain per deployed update is 1.8 to 3.1 times the naive rule's. The 95% upper bound on the false-improvement rate is below 5.5%: formal in (B) for independent tasks (3.56%), and conditional on the real data tested (0.33% to 5.40%).

items.title: Learning Sequential Decisions from Multiple Sources via Group-Robust Markov Decision Processes
items.summary: Learning a common policy from multiple source environments requires accounting for cross-source heterogeneity, and the offline setting introduces an additional challenge of limited data coverage. We formulate this problem as a distributionally robust Markov decision process under a shared linear MDP representation with source-specific transition and reward components. The uncertainty set is constructed through feature-wise mixtures of these components, yielding a $d$-rectangular structure that captures cross-source heterogeneity and admits a robust Bellman recursion. Building on this formulation, we develop Group-Robust Pessimistic Value Iteration (GR-PEVI), an offline policy-learning algorithm that combines feature-wise worst-case aggregation with a data-dependent pessimism penalty. Under a robust partial coverage condition, we establish finite-sample suboptimality guarantees for GR-PEVI and extend the analysis to clustered sources, characterizing the trade-off between the statistical gain from pooling similar sources and the approximation error induced by within-cluster heterogeneity. Simulation studies demonstrate the effectiveness of GR-PEVI, with empirical behavior consistent with the theoretical analysis. We apply GR-PEVI to a multi-source electronic health record study of multiple sclerosis treatment decisions to illustrate its use in a clinical setting.

items.title: Two-sample inference for sequence-derived feature distributions from deep sequencing data
items.summary: Many biological contexts involve heterogeneous populations of related molecular variants within a single individual. For example, some viral infections such as HIV-1 exhibit substantial diversity within a single host. Advances in sequencing technology now make it possible to characterize such populations by generating up to thousands of genetic sequences from a biological sample. In many settings, each sequence can be mapped to a numeric feature, such as Hamming distance to a reference sequence. This collection of feature values defines a one-dimensional distribution that characterizes individual-level viral diversity. When comparing these features across independent groups, past analyses have typically reduced each individual's data to a single summary value, such as the mean or mode. We propose a framework that retains the full individual-level distribution as the object of analysis. Drawing on existing tools from distributional data analysis, our framework uses Wasserstein barycenters to summarize the observed individual-level distributions within groups into a single representative distribution. These group barycenters are then compared using differences in quantiles and tested for equality. A practical challenge is that the number of sequences obtained, known as sequencing depth, can vary across biological samples. Through simulation studies, we examine when low sequencing depth can distort inference and present practical strategies for addressing these issues. We then illustrate the framework using data from the HIV-1 Antibody Mediated Prevention efficacy trials and a human B cell receptor sequencing study of vaccine-elicited immune responses. By using the entire collection of sequences for each individual, our approach can reveal group differences that may be obscured by single-number summary analyses.

items.title: Algorithmics for Graphical Separation Criteria
items.summary: Statistical graphical models are representations of the dependences between the components of a random vector. They encode these dependences via graphical separation criteria. We consider the algorithmic problem of checking separation statements for the various graph classes and separation criteria that have been developed by the community. We establish that all criteria we study can be checked by modular variations of reachability. For all separation criteria but $σ$-separation, this yields a linear-time algorithm. This is effectively the optimal attainable time since loading the graph itself is linear-time in the number of edges in the graph. Using the CIfly framework for deploying modular variations of reachability, we also provide R and Python code implementing our algorithms. We evaluate empirical runtime and scaling behavior in a simulation study.

items.title: Uniform Strong Convergence of Kernel-Type Estimators for m-LENQD Sequences with Applications
items.summary: In this paper, we firs tderiv eth eunifor mstron gconsistenc yan dth ecorrespondin gconvergence rates for kernel estimators of both the distribution function and the probability density function for sequences of m-linearly extended negative quadrant dependent (m-LENQD) random variables under mild regularity conditions. The obtained results significantl yimprov ean dexten dexisting ones in the literature. As their theoretical applications, we further establish the uniform strong consistency and convergence rates for estimators of the hazard rate function and the mode of the density function. Numerical simulations and a real data analysis are conducted to assess the finite- sample performance of the proposed estimators, confirmin gth easymptoti cpropertie sderive din the theoretical analysis.

items.title: Second-order Sinkhorn Geometry and $\sqrt{n}$-Inference
items.summary: The Sinkhorn divergence, a debiased form of entropic optimal transport, has been widely used in various scientific disciplines due to its computational and statistical tractability. Unlike the Wasserstein distance, however, the Sinkhorn divergence is not a metric and it does not naturally admit a formal Riemannian structure. These properties are central to many applications of optimal transport methods that utilize interpolation, barycentric averaging, parallel transport or other geometric operations. Recent work addresses these shortcomings by constructing a formal Riemannian tangent space and a metric tensor on the space of probability measures that quadratically approximates the Sinkhorn divergence. In this work, we extend this framework with two major threads of contributions. For a suitable class of finite-smoothness cost functions, we prove Hadamard differentiability of the Sinkhorn metric tensor and we derive the Levi-Civita covariant derivative in this geometry; we then use the covariant derivative to obtain the geodesic and parallel transport equations, each of which amount to an ODE on a fixed Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS) with smooth coefficients. Our second contribution is to linearize the solutions to the geodesic and parallel transport equations using standard tools from Banach space ODE theory. We show that under standard regularity conditions these linearizations imply $\sqrt{n}$-limiting Gaussian processes centered at population values for the plugin estimators of the exponential map, the logarithmic map, parallel transport and the induced Sinkhorn distance. Moreover, we show that the nonparametric bootstrap is consistent for all objects mentioned. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first $\sqrt{n}$--limit theorems and bootstrap consistency results for canonical geometric operations in a transport-based geometry on the space of probability measures.

items.title: Revenge of Monosemanticity: Neuron Specialization as a New Form of Feature Learning in MLPs
items.summary: Understanding how neural networks learn and organize features is central to understanding their behavior. Much existing theory of feature learning has focused on the emergence of a global low-dimensional representation. We show that this picture is incomplete. In regression problems with clustered data, we demonstrate that multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) develop specialized neurons: individual neurons become strongly aligned with specific features relevant to a particular region of the input space. A substantial fraction of these neurons exhibit monosemanticity: they activate predominantly on inputs from the corresponding cluster. Thus, rather than learning a single global low-dimensional representation, MLPs learn a collection of local low-dimensional representations. Furthermore, we show that this ability to specialize gives MLPs a provable data-efficiency advantage over feature-learning methods based on a global low-dimensional representation.

items.title: Advantage of Sample Complexity in Quantum PAC Learning Requires Inverse Access to State-Preparation Unitaries
items.summary: Whether quantum computation can reduce the amount of data required for conventional machine learning is a central problem in quantum machine learning. In probably approximately correct (PAC) learning, a learner receives training examples sampled from an unknown probability distribution. Quantum PAC learning extends this framework by allowing access to quantum examples, which are quantum states that coherently encode this distribution, or to unitaries that prepare quantum examples, with or without inverse access. When only copies of quantum examples are available, the optimal worst-case sample complexity asymptotically matches that of classical learning. In contrast, access to both a preparation unitary and its inverse can improve the accuracy dependence of query complexity. However, it has remained open whether access to the preparation unitary alone suffices for this improvement. In this work, we resolve this question by determining the optimal query complexity with forward-only access, taking the worst case over compatible preparation unitaries and their dimensions. In both realizable and agnostic PAC learning, this complexity matches, up to constant factors, the optimal sample complexity achievable with classical examples or copies of quantum examples. To prove these results, we construct, for any algorithm with forward-only access, a simulator that approximates the algorithm's Haar-averaged output state using as many copies of the prepared state as the algorithm makes queries. These results show that inverse access is essential for the known improvement in accuracy dependence in this worst-case setting. Beyond PAC learning, our reduction provides a general tool for transferring lower bounds for state copies to query lower bounds for forward-only access to the corresponding preparation unitaries.

items.title: Mirror Likelihood for Modeling Manifold Data with Application on Correlation Time Series
items.summary: Manifold-valued data arise in a wide range of scientific applications. Existing statistical methods typically follow either an intrinsic approach, which characterizes the manifold itself via quantities such as geodesic distance or the Fréchet mean, or an extrinsic approach, which embeds the manifold into an ambient Euclidean space, performs unconstrained statistical estimation, and projects the result back to the manifold. While the latter is conceptually and computationally simple, likelihood-based extrinsic solutions remain scarce, due to the lack of a general recipe for choosing an embedding map and for characterizing its impact on the transformed distribution. In this article, we tackle the problem using an augmented likelihood approach: we view the manifold-valued data as the Fenchel mirror map of a latent variable, which is nearly unconstrained, and model the latent variable with a canonical distribution, such as Gaussian. The key transform, the Fenchel mirror map, is a generalization of the Euclidean projection and can effectively map into the interior of the manifold. Taking a Bayesian approach, the proposed framework enjoys a generative model interpretation and an augmented likelihood free from intractable normalization constants, and it supports principled uncertainty quantification and flexible model-based extensions. We study the theoretical and computational properties of the framework and demonstrate its utility in analyzing neuroimaging data of high-dimensional correlation time series, where each correlation matrix is rank deficient.

items.title: Improved Regret Bounds for Gaussian Process Upper Confidence Bound in Bayesian Optimization
items.summary: This paper addresses the Bayesian optimization problem (also referred to as the Bayesian setting of the Gaussian process bandit), where the learner seeks to minimize the regret under a function drawn from a known Gaussian process (GP). Under a Matérn kernel with a certain degree of smoothness, we show that the Gaussian process upper confidence bound (GP-UCB) algorithm achieves $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ cumulative regret with high probability. Furthermore, our analysis yields $O(\sqrt{T \ln^2 T})$ regret under a squared exponential kernel. These results fill the gap between the existing regret upper bound for GP-UCB and the best-known bound provided by Scarlett (2018). The key idea in our proof is to capture the concentration behavior of the input sequence realized by GP-UCB, enabling a more refined analysis of the GP's information gain.

items.title: Orlicz-Sobolev with Musielak: An Efficient Regularization Approach for Graph-based IPM
items.summary: We study the Sobolev IPM problem for probability measures supported on a graph metric space, where critic function is constrained to lie within the unit ball defined by Sobolev norm. Sobolev IPM is intrinsically coupled with $L^p$ geometric structure within its definition, limiting its ability to incorporate other prior geometry beyond the $L^p$ paradigm. Conversely, the classic optimal transport is flexible, easy to adapt to various geometric structures by simply changing its ground cost. An important example is Orlicz-Wasserstein (OW) which utilizes \emph{Orlicz} geometric structure to generalize the $L^p$ within the standard $p$-order Wasserstein, and remarkably play a vital role to advance machine learning methodologies. Inspired by recent advantages of OW, in this work, we leverage a specific class of convex functions for Orlicz geometry to mitigate such limitation for Sobolev IPM, and propose the generalized Sobolev IPM (GSI). Our GSI approach encompasses Sobolev IPM as a special case while accommodating diverse geometric priors beyond $L^p$. It however brings up significant computational hurdles that compound those already notoriously inherent in Sobolev IPM. To address these challenges, we theoretically establish a novel connection between \emph{Orlicz-Sobolev} norm and \emph{Musielak} norm which facilitates a novel efficient regularization for GSI. By further exploiting the underlying graph structure, we show that the regularized GSI reduces to a simple univariate optimization problem, achieving notably computational efficiency, enabling its usage in practical applications. We empirically illustrate that the regularized GSI is several-order faster than the popular OW in computation, and its performances compare favorably to other transport baselines for comparing graph-based measures in document classification and topological data analysis.

items.title: Fixed-Horizon Error Rates for Array-RQMC Metropolis-Hastings
items.summary: This paper studies randomised quasi-Monte Carlo (RQMC) methods for Metropolis--Hastings (MH) algorithms, whose accept--reject discontinuity complicates RQMC analysis. To circumvent some of these complications, we study Array-RQMC for MH, with $N$ replicated chains evolved over a fixed time horizon $T$, where we make use of Hilbert sorting for joint multidimensional updates at each step. For one-dimensional MH and bounded-variation test functions, we prove a sampling mean squared error bound of $\mathcal O_T(N^{-4/3})$ relative to the finite-horizon expectation. For product targets, coordinatewise Array-RQMC Metropolis-within-Gibbs retains this exponent for additive marginal bounded-variation tests, with constants that may depend on dimension. With Gaussian random-walk proposals, the bounds extend to scalar and additive marginal polynomials with an additional factor $(\log N)^\ell$, where $\ell$ is the maximum polynomial degree. For joint updates in state dimension $p$ using $p$ proposal uniforms, we provide a conditional $\mathcal O_T(N^{-1-1/(p+2)})$ framework under regularity assumptions that are not verified for the joint multidimensional examples. Numerical experiments support the verified one-dimensional theory and demonstrate variance reduction for joint Hilbert-sorted updates, including Bayesian logistic regression, while illustrating the limitations of these gains as dimension increases.

items.title: Finite-population inference for cross-fitted estimators of treatment contrasts in stratified multistage surveys
items.summary: Health surveys often sample clusters within strata and then individuals within clusters, and flexible outcome and treatment models complicate inference for adjusted contrasts from such surveys. We establish finite-population limit theory for survey-weighted augmented inverse-probability-weighted estimation within the double machine learning framework, using cross-fitting that keeps whole clusters together; a cross-fitted targeted maximum likelihood estimator inherits the results under additional targeting conditions. With first-stage clusters drawn by simple random sampling without replacement within strata, the theory allows arbitrary within-cluster dependence, appreciable sampling fractions, and many small strata, a few large strata, or both. Under bounded cluster sizes, a cluster-generation model and nuisance convergence-rate conditions, the estimator is asymptotically normal about the finite-population contrast, and a stability property derived from the cluster model controls the cross-fitting error without entropy conditions. The stratified ultimate-cluster variance estimator, without a first-stage finite-population correction, consistently estimates a with-replacement variance that is at least the without-replacement design variance of the normal limit, so the resulting intervals are asymptotically conservative, and exact when the excess is negligible. In simulations, near-nominal or higher coverage coexisted, in different settings, with remainder diagnostics above the study's negligibility benchmark and with inaccurate standard errors. In three Service Provision Assessment surveys from Malawi and Haiti, each frame treated as a fixed population and resampled 500 times, mean reported standard errors were 4%-20% larger than the empirical standard deviations, while coverage of whole-frame reference values was near or above nominal.

items.title: On The Variability of Concept Activation Vectors
items.summary: One of the most pressing challenges in artificial intelligence is to make models more transparent to their users. Recently, explainable artificial intelligence has come up with numerous methods to tackle this challenge. A promising avenue is to use concept-based explanations, that is, high-level concepts instead of plain feature importance scores. Among this class of methods, Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs, Kim et al., 2018) stand out as one of the main protagonists. One interesting aspect of CAVs is that their computation requires sampling random examples from the train set. Therefore, the actual vectors obtained may vary depending on the randomness of this sampling. In this paper, we propose a fine-grained theoretical analysis of CAV construction in order to quantify their variability. Our results, confirmed by experiments on several real-life datasets of four different modalities, point to an universal result: the variance of CAVs declines roughly as $1/N$, where $N$ is the number of random examples. Based on this, we give practical recommendations for a resource-efficient application of the method.

items.title: Speed-accuracy relations for diffusion models: Wisdom from nonequilibrium thermodynamics and optimal transport
items.summary: We discuss a connection between a generative model, called the diffusion model, and nonequilibrium thermodynamics for the Fokker-Planck equation, called stochastic thermodynamics. Using techniques from stochastic thermodynamics, we derive the speed-accuracy relations for diffusion models, which are inequalities that relate the accuracy of data generation to the entropy production rate. This relation can be interpreted as the speed of the diffusion dynamics in the absence of the non-conservative force. From a stochastic thermodynamic perspective, our results provide quantitative insight into how best to generate data in diffusion models. The optimal learning protocol is introduced by the geodesic of space of the 2-Wasserstein distance in optimal transport theory. We numerically illustrate the validity of the speed-accuracy relations for diffusion models with different noise schedules and different data. We numerically discuss our results for optimal and suboptimal learning protocols. We also demonstrate the applicability of our results to data generation from the real-world image datasets.

items.title: On the Optimal Sample Complexity of Offline Multi-Armed Bandits with KL Regularization
items.summary: Kullback-Leibler (KL) regularization is widely used in offline decision-making and offers several benefits, motivating recent work on the sample complexity of offline learning with respect to KL-regularized performance metrics. Nevertheless, the exact sample complexity of KL-regularized offline learning remains largely from fully characterized. In this paper, we study this question in the setting of multi-armed bandits (MABs). We provide a sharp analysis of KL-PCB (Zhao et al., 2026), showing that it achieves a sample complexity of $\tilde{O}(ηSAC^{π^*}/ε)$ under large regularization $η= \tilde{O}(ε^{-1})$, and a sample complexity of $\tildeΩ(SAC^{π^*}/ε^2)$ under small regularization $η= \tildeΩ(ε^{-1})$, where $η$ is the regularization parameter, $S$ is the number of contexts, $A$ is the number of arms, $C^{π^*}$ policy coverage coefficient at the optimal policy $π^*$, $ε$ is the desired sub-optimality, and $\tilde{O}$ and $\tildeΩ$ hide all poly-logarithmic factors. We further provide a pair of sharper sample complexity lower bounds, which matches the upper bounds over the entire range of regularization strengths. Overall, our results provide a nearly complete characterization of offline multi-armed bandits with KL regularization.

items.title: Many Hands Make Light Work: Long-Term Effect Inference for the Experiment Reservoir
items.summary: The surrogate index method is the modern standard for estimation of long-term effects in a designed experiment using only short-term outcomes. This method relies on the surrogacy and comparability assumptions which may be violated in practice leading to estimation bias. We propose a new method called Experiment Reservoir Surrogate (ERS) which leverages a reservoir of historical long-term experiments that is common in large-scale experimentation platforms. ERS avoids the surrogacy assumption by predicting the long-term average treatment effect directly, and relaxes the comparability assumption by matching to similar historical experiments, without requiring every experiment in the reservoir to be comparable to the target experiment. Moreover, ERS is memory-efficient, as it only requires aggregate data for each time period, instead of raw individual-level data. We theoretically justify the improved efficiency of ERS and demonstrate the improvement empirically on a reservoir of experiments from the online platform DoorDash.

items.title: Estimating the Effect of a Low Nicotine Standard on Smoking Behavior in the U.S. Population
items.summary: In January of 2025, the FDA announced a proposed rule to set a nationwide nicotine standard of 0.7 mg/cigarette that would reduce nicotine levels in cigarettes by 95$\%$. Past trials comparing very-low nicotine content (VLNC) cigarettes and normal nicotine content (NNC) cigarettes consistently found randomization to receive VLNC cigarettes reduces cigarette consumption. However, these results are not intrinsically generalizable, as the trials exhibited partial treatment non-adherence and were not designed as representative samples of the United States (U.S.) population of people who smoke (PWS). Existing transportability methods do not account for non-adherence or target a different estimand. Additionally, non-adherence cannot be directly observed and must be estimated using biomarkers of nicotine exposure, and different biomarkers were collected across trials. To estimate the effect of full adherence to a low nicotine standard in the U.S. population of PWS, we develop a novel inverse odds weighting estimator for transporting an intervention's effect to a fully adherent target population, and propose a bivariate mixture model approach for estimating adherence using biomarkers that allows partial missingness in one of the biomarkers. Finally, we use our method to transport inferences from seven trials investigating VLNC cigarettes to a representative sample of U.S. PWS.

items.title: Leveraging Large Language Models to Improve Precision in Randomized Controlled Trials
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in statistical research and applications. However, they are also notorious for unreliable or biased information. Here, we explore whether LLMs can be used to improve the precision of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in a safe and rigorous way. We consider two pathways for incorporating LLM assistance: (1) using LLMs to transform non-standard covariates, such as text, into numerical representations, and (2) leveraging the general knowledge embedded in LLMs to generate predicted outcomes. Although external data sources have been leveraged to improve precision before, the value added by LLM-generated predictions through these pathways remains an open question. We develop a pipeline for generally leveraging LLMs in this context and apply it to three different case studies. We find that we are able to safely improve precision, primarily through transforming non-standard covariates, but that LLMs also possess general knowledge that is useful in some contexts.

items.title: Latent Nonlinear Denoising Score Matching for Enhanced Learning of Structured Distributions
items.summary: Score-based generative models commonly employ linear forward diffusions with Gaussian reference distributions, limiting their ability to directly incorporate structural information into the noising dynamics. We introduce latent nonlinear denoising score matching (LNDSM), which combines nonlinear, structure-informed latent diffusions with the variational autoencoder (VAE) training framework. In our construction, the forward diffusion is designed to admit a prescribed reference distribution, such as a Gaussian mixture model, that reflects qualitative features of the latent data distribution. We derive a computable approximation to a cross-entropy upper bound in the VAE objective using Euler-Maruyama discretization and the resulting Gaussian conditional transitions. To stabilize training, we remove two zero-mean control variates whose variances become large for small time steps. The resulting objective enables joint training of the encoder, decoder, and latent score network. Numerical experiments on benchmark image datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of LNDSM in learning structured distributions, outperforming conventional latent score-based generative modeling in sample quality and mode balance across several settings, while achieving improved training efficiency. These results highlight the potential of nonlinear, structure-informed latent diffusions for generative modeling.

items.title: Confidence Is Not a Promise: A Reference Audit of Typed Decision Models
items.summary: Typed decision models return a probability distribution over options supplied by the caller, and software tends to act on that number as if it were a guarantee. We measure what it licenses, comparing the open-weight Laya, in five checkpoints, with Jev 1.13, available only through an API. A probability licenses a statement about groups of decisions, not about one decision, and a gate that promises an accuracy among the cases it decides alone keeps that promise only with a lower bound checked on data like its traffic. Across 190 exchangeable evaluations, a threshold chosen by point estimate breaks the promise in 147, Learn then Test keeps it in all of them, and a Beta lower-bound rule decides more items on average than Learn then Test in 128 and fewer in none, without its guarantee. Calibrated in English, Jev keeps a promise of 95% in 8 of 51 locales. Ordinary typing noise breaks a promise calibrated on clean text, and, in exploratory runs, training with noise raises the noisy accuracy with no loss on clean text. In four further domains, a fine-tuned Laya needs from 250 to 8,000 labels to be non-inferior to Jev, and does not get there on LIAR2. Under drift, the preregistered claim for a Bayesian retraining loop is not supported: the loop avoids needless retraining where the change does not degrade the model, at a cost equivalent to recalibration alone, and re-qualifying the threshold in every window keeps the promise more often where it does. On the monthly series of M3, neither decider predicts the direction of the next value better than a constant answer. Confidence separates right from wrong answers with an AUROC from 0.80 to 0.96, but it does not select faithful explanations, and exact coalition games of single decisions show what an explanation can still say through an API that rounds to two decimals. We release the frozen answers with a datasheet, a promise check and the code.

items.title: Simulation-based Criticism of Complex Biological Models with Neural Evidence Estimation
items.summary: In statistical modeling, the likelihood is the basis for both inference and criticism, which constitute the two stages of data analysis. However, many realistic scientific models lack computationally tractable likelihoods. Increasingly, these are implemented as computer simulations. New deep learning-based methods for simulation-based inference (SBI) have demonstrated the ability to efficiently and accurately calibrate complex simulation models. However, in this setting, the standard tools for comparing models and assessing their potential limitations are often unavailable. We propose a new method for simulation-based model criticism, Neural Evidence Estimation. NEE trains a normalizing flow on simulated data to learn an estimate of the marginal likelihood (a.k.a. evidence). These estimates can be used to diagnose model misspecification and perform model comparison without evaluating (or approximating) a model's likelihood. Compared to related techniques designed for either of these tasks, NEE is quick, robust, and modular. We demonstrate our methodology through applications to infectious disease modeling. Here, model criticism is difficult yet imperative: infectious disease modelers often face a choice among several plausible models featuring intractable likelihoods. We first validate NEE's ability to discern incorrect transmission models through simulation experiments. We then perform data analysis of a historic multi-wave influenza epidemic, where we use SBI and NEE to rigorously compare several competing mechanistic theories of reinfection. Overall, NEE provides a unifying framework for simulation-based criticism, advances efficient multi-model data analysis, and helps improve the reliability of SBI.

items.title: Contextual Factors Behind Income Inequality: A Predictive Analysis
items.summary: Income inequality remains a central concern in economics and public policy, yet conclusions about its predictors often depend on both the factors considered and the measure of inequality used. This paper examines the predictive importance of a broad set of indicators covering structural factors, capital structure, financial-sector development, political institutions, regional classification, human capital, globalization, and technology. Using data for 88 countries from 1970 to 2017 and six inequality measures from the World Income Inequality Database (WIID), we apply a machine learning approach to assess the relative predictive importance of 35 candidate indicators across alternative income inequality measures. The analysis proceeds in three stages: a full specification including all candidate indicators, a category-representative specification with one common indicator from each conceptual category, and an inequality-specific specification allowing the most predictive indicator within each category to vary across inequality measures. Regional classification is the dominant predictor across all specifications and inequality measures, although its broad nature prevents identification of the specific regional characteristics underlying this result. Political and technology indicators provide the most consistent additional predictive information, whereas the importance of human capital, financial development, and globalization varies across inequality measures. Technology is particularly informative for top-income concentration, while returns to capital are more relevant for measures capturing gaps between the upper and lower parts of the income distribution.

items.title: Unifying Sparse Estimation of Precision and Covariance Matrices
items.summary: Penalized maximum likelihood is a widely used approach to estimate a sparse precision or a sparse covariance matrix. A zero in the precision matrix encodes a conditional independence and a zero in the covariance matrix a marginal independence, and the two estimators have been developed separately, each with its own algorithm. We show that these two problems can be unified via a single reparametrization of the last column of either matrix. This reparametrization decouples the likelihood function for each problem to a one-dimensional minimization followed by a penalized multiple regression. Our approach applies to any penalty that is separable in the off-diagonal entries and linear on the diagonal. When the penalty is the $\ell_1$ norm, it unifies the graphical Lasso and the covariance graphical Lasso algorithms.

items.title: Directional Statistics on Circles and Spheres: A New Angle on Data
items.summary: Two compass bearings near north can have an ordinary arithmetic mean pointing south: the difficulty is that angles live on a circle, not a straight line. Using real wind observations, diffusion-MRI orientations, and geometric examples from machine learning, this article introduces circular and axial averages, directional variability, and probability models on circles and spheres. The guiding principle is to identify the geometry and symmetries of the observations before choosing a statistical method.

items.title: Relaxed MEMs: Enhancing Borrowing in Multisource Exchangeability Models for Small Sample Applications
items.summary: Information sharing in clinical trials provides a promising way to increase trial efficiency, specifically in rare disease settings where sample sizes are small. Multisource Exchangeability Modeling (MEM) is a method that incorporates historical data from potentially multiple data sources, such as past trials, by exploring all possible configurations of exchangeability and provides a weight estimate for each configuration, allowing the user to quantify how much is being borrowed from each source. While MEMs have previously been shown to be asymptotically consistent, small sample sizes introduce uncertainty that naturally limits the amount of borrowing MEMs can facilitate. The proposed ``relaxed MEMs'' provide a mathematical framework for relaxing or removing those limits and allowing greater borrowing even in small-sample settings. Several relaxed MEM versions are proposed, and all strategies provide enhanced borrowing with minimal sacrifice in the bias and variance of the mean estimates. Specifically, the maximum absolute mean bias was 3.5\% (0.035) of the true mean in the two source continuous outcome settings and 6.4\% (0.032) of the true proportion in the two source binary outcome settings (absolute mean bias was 1.4\% (0.014) and 3.6\% (0.018), respectively, for traditional MEMs) and variance decreased relative to traditional MEMs across all exchangeable and small difference scenarios. The methods were then demonstrated using two endpoints from a series of phase II trials in cystic fibrosis.

items.title: Improving causal inference in interrupted time series analysis: the triple difference design
items.summary: Background: Interrupted time series analysis (ITSA) is widely used to evaluate health policy and intervention effects. While multiple-group ITSA (MG-ITSA) improves causal inference by incorporating a control group, residual confounding from unmeasured time-varying factors may remain. The triple-difference interrupted time series (DDD-ITSA) design extends this approach by adding a second control group to further isolate treatment effects, but it remains underutilized and lacks formal guidance. Methods: We formalize the DDD-ITSA framework, specify the regression model, define key parameters for estimating level and trend effects, and clarify interpretation of the triple-difference estimand. We illustrate the approach using a worked example evaluating California's Proposition 99 cigarette tax and its impact on per-capita cigarette sales. Results: In the example, all groups were balanced on pre-intervention level and trend. The triple-difference estimand indicated a statistically significant annual reduction of -1.76 per-capita cigarette packs in California relative to the secondary control (P = 0.020; 95 percent CI: -3.24, -0.28), consistent with results from the primary comparison. Differences between control groups were not significant. Conclusions: DDD-ITSA strengthens causal inference when two-group comparisons may be confounded by leveraging an additional control group to remove remaining biases and assess heterogeneity. Implementation is facilitated by updates to the itsa Stata package. Careful attention to control selection, baseline balance, and autocorrelation remains essential.

items.title: Approximation Families and the Statistical Efficiency of Denoising Score Matching
items.summary: We study score matching over finite-dimensional approximation spaces generated by gradients of eigenfunctions of the infinitesimal generator of a forward diffusion. We compare polynomial approximation under one-dimensional Ornstein-Uhlenbeck flow with trigonometric-polynomial approximation under heat flow on the torus. In the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck setting, we show that for every non-Gaussian initial distribution uniformly comparable to the standard Gaussian, the asymptotic score-estimation variance grows exponentially along a subsequence of polynomial degrees. Averaging the score-matching loss under the diffusion semigroup, which we call operator-informed score matching (OISM), reduces the variance at each fixed degree but does not eliminate this exponential instability at sufficiently small times. A local minimax lower bound shows that the same high-degree dependence arises when estimating the polynomial projection of the score, rather than being an artifact of OISM. In contrast, under heat flow on the torus, OISM over trigonometric polynomials admits finite-sample control of the score error along the forward diffusion and yields the classical minimax rate for estimating sufficiently smooth densities under expected Kullback-Leibler loss.

items.title: Computational and Statistical Guarantees of the c-Rectified flow
items.summary: Recently, rectified flow has emerged as a fundamental framework for large-scale image generation, powering state-of-the-art systems such as FLUX.1 and Stable Diffusion 3. Despite its remarkable empirical success, the computational and statistical guarantees of iterative rectified flow have remained largely unexplored. We address this problem by studying c-rectified flow, a cost-aware class of rectified flow that projects velocity fields onto a gradient class while preserving endpoint marginals. The ordinary rectified flow can fail to recover the optimal transport coupling: in a Gaussian case study, the iteration converges to the optimal coupling if and only if the source and target covariance matrices commute. More generally, for a Gaussian to log-concave coupling, the ordinary rectified flow can reach a fixed point after one step from independent initialization. In contrast, under suitable regularity and uniform-integrability assumptions, iterative c-rectified flow always converges to the optimal transport coupling. We further establish quantitative one-step contraction and exponential convergence guarantees under projection-stability assumptions for both quadratic and strongly convex displacement costs. Finally, under a Hölder ball assumption, we develop new minimax-optimal score estimation rates and show that, when combined with iterative c-rectified flow, they yield a rate-optimal estimator of the optimal transport for the dimension \(d \ge 3\) and a nearly parametric rate for \(d=1,2\).

items.title: Parametric Rates for Nonparametric Conditional-Moment Bilevel Optimization
items.summary: We study functional bilevel optimization with conditional moments, where plug-in hypergradients can inherit first-order errors from nonparametrically learned conditional expectations. We introduce OBiGrad, an orthogonalized hypergradient estimator whose bias is a product of nuisance errors.
