China began a gradual delayed-retirement (GDR) reform in 2025, raising statutory retirement ages on different schedules for men, female cadres, and female workers across birth cohorts. To evaluate its effects on older individuals and within the family, we develop a model of older adults' retirement, intergenerational transfers, and adult children's fertility decisions, with parameters estimated via fuzzy regression discontinuity at the pre-2025 statutory retirement ages. Counterfactual simulations show that, for mature reform cohorts, the GDR reform increases older employment and monetary transfers to adult children but reduces grandparental childcare. Because the reduction in childcare outweighs the increase in monetary transfers, fertility and older adults' welfare decline, with particularly large losses among lower-income women. Fully flexible retirement, mandatory partial retirement, and mandatory full-time work do not raise employment without similarly reducing fertility and welfare. Childcare subsidies can offset the declines in fertility and welfare, while restricting eligibility to women or lower-income women requires higher subsidy rates but reduces average fiscal expenditure. These findings suggest that evaluations of retirement policy should consider not only its direct effects on older adults' labor supply, but also its fertility effects through intergenerational transfers; childcare support can help mitigate these negative intergenerational effects of delayed retirement.

items.title: AI-Augmented Research: Free to Write, Costly to Read
items.summary: We study a model in which artificial intelligence lowers the cost of writing faster than the cost of reading. Authors differ in reputation, and time-constrained readers, such as referees, choose between ignoring, verifying, and trusting papers. As writing costs fall, the band of verified papers shrinks: outsiders are no longer read, and established authors are no longer checked. In the ``costless writing limit,'' the share of verified papers vanishes, and a paper's impact depends on its author's reputation alone. Readers can escape the flood by asking AI to summarize the literature. These summaries aggregate papers reliably only if their errors are sufficiently independent. Once the share of papers written with the same AI exceeds a threshold, summaries inherit the AI's errors, and AI review filters out the original research that could correct them.

items.title: Jawboning the Fed: Do Markets Listen When Administrations Talk?
items.summary: We provide the first systematic evidence on whether financial markets price political pressure on the Federal Reserve as a signal of future monetary policy. Using approximately four decades of Reuters newswire articles from 1988 to 2025, classified by an open-weight large language model ensemble into dovish and hawkish pressure, we estimate the daily response of interest rate expectations across the term structure, the US dollar, inflation compensation, and market volatility. Dovish pressure lowers near-term rate expectations by roughly one basis point per pressure event---equivalent to a four-percent increase in the implied probability of a rate cut at the next FOMC meeting---with the effect decaying monotonically and vanishing beyond the three-month horizon. Hawkish pressure has no detectable effect. Furthermore, excluding the Trump presidencies does not weaken the estimate, ruling out the possibility that the result is confined to an idiosyncratic recent episode. The response is accompanied by dollar depreciation, with stable inflation compensation and market volatility. We interpret the pattern as markets pricing anticipated monetary accommodation, rather than a credibility tax on the nominal anchor.

items.title: Dynamic Mortality Forecasting via Mixed-Frequency State-Space Models
items.summary: High-frequency death counts are now widely available and contain timely information about intra-year mortality dynamics, but most stochastic mortality models are still estimated on annual data and therefore update only when annual totals are released. We propose a mixed-frequency state-space (MF--SS) extension of the Lee--Carter framework that jointly uses annual mortality rates and monthly death counts. The two series are linked through a shared latent monthly mortality factor, with the annual period factor defined as the intra-year average of the monthly factors. The latent monthly factor follows a seasonal ARIMA process, and parameters are estimated by maximum likelihood using an EM algorithm with Kalman filtering and smoothing. This setup enables real-time intra-year updates of the latent state and forecasts as new monthly observations arrive without re-estimating model parameters. Using U.S. data for ages 20--90 over 1999--2019, we evaluate intra-year annual nowcasts and one- to five-year-ahead forecasts. The MF--SS model produces both a direct annual forecast and an annual forecast implied by aggregating monthly projections. In our application, the aggregated monthly forecast is typically more accurate. Incorporating monthly information substantially improves intra-year annual nowcasts, especially after the first few months of the year. As a benchmark, we also fit separate annual and monthly Lee--Carter models and combine their forecasts using temporal reconciliation. Reconciliation improves these independent forecasts but adds little to MF--SS forecasts, consistent with MF--SS pooling information across frequencies during estimation. The MF--SS aggregated monthly forecasts generally outperform both unreconciled and temporally reconciled Lee--Carter forecasts and produce more cautious predictive intervals than the reconciled Lee--Carter approach.

items.title: GenAI-Assisted Writing and Academic Performance: Evidence from the Social and Behavioral Sciences
items.summary: This paper studies how Generative AI (GenAI)-assisted writing is associated with peer-reviewed publication output and journal placement in the social and behavioral sciences. We select lexical markers whose frequency rose sharply after ChatGPT's release in late 2022 and classify authors as GenAI-assisted writers when the share of these markers in their papers' titles and abstracts rises relative to their own pre-release baseline. Using matched author-level panel data and a difference-in-differences design, we estimate a 72% increase in publication output among GenAI-assisted writers relative to matched comparison authors in 2025. Across alternative specifications, the estimates range from roughly 52% to 88%. Mean journal placement based on the SCImago Journal Rank (SJR) improves by roughly 1%, but this modest increase is less consistent across different specifications. Within authors' annual publication portfolios, the highest placement improves by 5%, whereas the lowest declines by 3%. However, only the improvement at the top persists once the annual number of publications is held constant. The increase in output is accompanied by an expansion of collaboration networks and a rise in single-authored publications. Productivity gains are largest among early-career researchers and authors from countries linguistically distant from English, groups likely to face greater writing-related barriers to publication. The results suggest that GenAI-assisted writing may lower these barriers and increase researchers' capacity to bring more projects to publication.

items.title: Rational Learning One Step Off the Path
items.summary: We study how endogenous learning shapes beliefs and strategies in extensive-form games. We adopt the overlapping-generations model of \citet{FL1993}, in which finitely lived Bayesian agents are randomly matched, observe only the outcomes of their own matches, and choose dynamically optimal strategies. We study limiting strategy profiles in steady states as agents become arbitrarily long lived and patient. We show that learning disciplines beliefs and strategies in subgames reached after a single deviation from the path of play. In particular, we establish the converse of \citet{FL2006}, showing that such limiting strategy profiles must be path-equivalent to subgame-confirmed equilibria.

items.title: Short-Run Multi-Outcome Effects of Nightlife Regulation in San Juan
items.summary: I evaluate San Juan, Puerto Rico's late-night alcohol sales ordinance using a multi-outcome synthetic control that pools economic and public-safety series. I show that a common-weight estimator clarifies mechanisms under low-rank outcome structure. I find economically meaningful reallocations in targeted sectors -- restaurants and bars, gasoline and convenience, and hospitality employment -- while late-night public disorder arrests and violent crime show no clear departures from pre-policy trends. The short post-policy window and small donor pool limit statistical power; joint conformal and permutation tests do not reject the null at conventional thresholds. I therefore emphasize effect magnitudes, temporal persistence, and pre-trend fit over formal significance. Code and diagnostics are available for replication.

items.title: SAUSS: Stochastic Approximation with Unbiased Simulated Scores for Limited Dependent Variable Models
items.summary: Simulated maximum likelihood is widely used in latent-variable models where likelihood evaluation requires intractable integrals or probabilities. With a fixed number of simulation draws, its estimating equation is generally biased. We develop Stochastic Approximation with Unbiased Simulated Scores (SAUSS), combining score simulation with stochastic gradient descent. The Hajivassiliou--McFadden identity, an instance of Fisher's identity, expresses the likelihood score as the conditional expectation of the complete-data score given the observed data. Exact conditional draws yield an unbiased simulated score for any fixed number of draws. The estimator averages stochastic gradient iterates computed using mini-batches of fixed size regardless of sample size, avoiding repeated full-sample likelihood evaluations. Under local regularity and initialization conditions, we establish asymptotic normality and a functional central limit theorem for the partial-sum process of the iterates under multi-pass sampling from an observed sample. These results support plug-in and random-scaling confidence intervals that remain asymptotically valid when algorithmic uncertainty is non-negligible relative to sampling uncertainty. We develop multinomial probit as a leading application. In simulations and two applications, SAUSS returns estimates in every reported run, including cases where the simulated maximum likelihood implementation returns none. When both return estimates, SAUSS gives comparable estimates in less time.

items.title: Execution and Evaluation: Task Content, Labor Demand, and the Evaluator Pipeline
items.summary: Measures of occupational AI exposure ask whether machines can perform a task, not which function the human supplies. I distinguish execution, producing a first-pass output, from evaluation, judging whether it is correct, and make the distinction measurable by scoring all 19,265 O*NET task statements under fixed rubrics. The execution score is reproducible across model coders and O*NET vintages. In a 200-task random audit it correlates 0.81 with the mean of four blinded human coders. It predicts each held-out coder's peers better than that coder does, though the coders disagree substantially among themselves. It adds only modest power beyond O*NET's evaluation activities. Employment growth is lower in execution-heavy white-collar occupations in every window since 2012; the gradient shows no post-2022 break and lies largely between occupational families. The Eloundou exposure gradient is steeper in 2022--2025 than in the pandemic window, but the design does not establish an AI effect. A near-term seniority test is null. If evaluative judgment is itself produced by execution practice, the supply of evaluators falls only after a cohort lag; that prediction remains untested.

items.title: Working with AI: Measuring the Applicability of Generative AI to Occupations
items.summary: With generative AI emerging as a general-purpose technology, understanding its economic effects is among society's most pressing questions. Earlier work on AI impact largely relied on predictions of AI capabilities or focused narrowly on individual firms. Drawing instead on real-world AI usage, we analyze a dataset of 200k anonymized conversations with Microsoft Bing Copilot to measure AI applicability to occupations. We use an LLM-based pipeline to classify the O*NET work activities assisted or performed by AI in each conversation. We find that the most common and successful AI-assisted work activities involve information work--the creation, processing, and communication of information. At the occupation level, we find widespread AI applicability cutting across sectors, as most occupations have information work components. Our methodology also allows us to predict which occupations are more likely to delegate tasks to AI and which are more likely to use AI to assist existing workflows. Finally, we see an increase in occupation-level AI applicability over our 9-month data period, driven primarily by people using AI for more varied tasks. AI applicability scores and component usage and success metrics are available at https://github.com/microsoft/working-with-ai.

items.title: Parallel Trends as a Spectrum
items.summary: Difference-in-differences (DiD) designs are typically used to identify and estimate average causal effects, even though treatment can affect the entire outcome distribution. This has led to a growing interest in distributional DiD methods. However, identifying the full counterfactual distribution requires a parallel trends assumption on the entire distributional dynamics, which can be too strong in practice. We address this problem by introducing a spectrum of identifying restrictions that lie between the average and fully distributional DiD by imposing parallel trends on $L$-moments. This corresponds to a basis expansion of the distributional dynamics. Importantly, each $L$-moment is interpretable as familiar distributional components: location, dispersion, skewness, kurtosis, etc. Researchers can pick and choose which features they want to target. For example, the second $L$-moment identifies the Gini mean difference, but does not require imposing mean-level or higher-order parallel trends. Taking a collection of $L$-moments can approximate distributional dynamics under weaker conditions since it leaves untargeted components unrestricted. We develop conditions under which higher-order $L$-moments decay, efficient estimators, and simultaneous inference across growing collections of moments. We demonstrate the benefits of our framework by exploring distributional changes to healthcare spending after the rollout of Medicare Part D.

items.title: Blameocracy: Causal Rhetoric in Politics
items.summary: Democratic politics requires voters to infer how political actions map into outcomes, yet these causal links are often unclear, giving politicians scope to shape voters' causal accounts. This paper studies the supply and returns of causal rhetoric in politics: politicians' language linking political actions to outcomes through blame and credit. We fine-tune a language model to measure its use in 4.2 million congressional tweets spanning 2012--2023. Causal rhetoric is central to politicians' communication: it accounts for more than one third of tweets, is the language of political disagreement, and rises over time. The political returns of causal rhetoric are concentrated in blame. Combining campaign contributions with quasi-exogenous geographic variation in Twitter adoption, we find that exposure to blame has the largest effects on small donations. Using voting intentions from survey data and an event-study design around blame-only and credit-only days, we find that politicians' support rises after blame-only days. Finally, causal rhetoric appears rarely supported by economic knowledge, particularly blame.

items.title: Carbon Regulation and Competition in the European Airline Industry
items.summary: The European Union Emissions Trading System is set to substantially increase the effective carbon price faced by airlines. We estimate a two-stage model of airline competition with endogenous product entry, direct departure frequencies, and pricing. Impacts are highly asymmetric across carrier types and market segments. Consumer surplus declines by up to 34% overall and up to 95% in medium- and long-haul markets. Short-haul markets gain welfare as airlines reallocate capacity toward shorter routes. Airline profits decline by 1--42%, but carbon tax revenue of $1.9--2.9 billion and the social value of avoided emissions of $2.7--4.0 billion more than offset private-surplus losses.

items.title: Dynamic Test Design
items.summary: We study dynamic test design under the threat of manipulation. At each instant, a principal who cannot commit to future actions chooses whether to hire an agent, fire him, or continue costly probation by designing a test. The test provides information about the agent's persistent type, which is either good or bad. After observing the test choice, the bad type can exert costly effort to manipulate the evidence and mimic the good type. Deterring manipulation imposes an endogenous information budget that limits how intensively the principal can test. We show that, except at beliefs that remain unchanged in the absence of news, equilibrium tests are one-sided: they generate only passes, which trigger hiring, or only failures, which trigger firing. Equilibrium outcomes feature either correct hiring and firing decisions after costly delay or immediate decisions that risk misallocation. With commitment, the principal instead keeps the test constant throughout probation, even when she is nearly certain of the agent's type.

items.title: How Much Weak Overlap Can Doubly Robust T-Statistics Handle?
items.summary: Propensity scores near zero or one can make standard confidence intervals undercover. Econometric theory has targeted the Average Treatment Effect (ATE) under such weak overlap using nonstandard estimators or intervals. Practice has instead favored fixed thresholding rules that restore asymptotic normality by discarding extreme-propensity units for whom treatment may matter most. I show that standard t-tests for the ATE remain valid even when overlap is so weak that every regular estimator has infinite asymptotic variance. The key is to threshold the usual doubly robust estimator aggressively enough to control bias among unthresholded observations, but mildly enough to control bias from thresholding. I provide sufficient conditions for such thresholds to exist, and propose an adaptive rule of thumb to achieve coverage without knowing the weak overlap degree. In a canonical application, fixed trimming excludes 18% of the sample; the adaptive procedure estimates the resulting bias at five percent of the effect.

items.title: Marital Sorting, Household Inequality and Selection
items.summary: Using CPS data for 1976 to 2025, we explore how wage inequality has evolved for married couples with both spouses working full time full year, and its impact on household income inequality. We also investigate how marriage sorting patterns have changed over this period. To determine the factors driving income inequality we estimate a model explaining the joint distribution of couples' wages that accounts for spouses' employment decisions. This requires a multivariate distribution regression model that incorporates a double selection rule. We find that income inequality has increased for these households and increased wage sorting has exacerbated the inequality resulting from individual wage growth. We find that positive sorting partially reflects the correlation across unobservables influencing the wages of both members of the marriage. We decompose the changes in sorting patterns over the 50-year sample into structural, composition and selection effects and find that the increase in positive sorting primarily reflects the increased skill premia for both observed and unobserved characteristics.

items.title: Affirmative Action's Cumulative Fractional Assignments
items.summary: India's reservation policy entitles designated groups to fixed fractions of faculty positions. Positions are indivisible, arrive over time across departments, and appointments are irreversible. We show that no rule can keep cumulative reserved counts nondecreasing while rounding entitlements to adjacent integers at both the department and university levels; university-level compliance forces department-level errors that grow without bound. This impossibility explains why both solutions practiced in India provoked litigation and protests. A random-roster solution preserves irreversibility and department-level compliance, matches entitlements in expectation, and concentrates university-level errors. Dropping cumulative accounting restores exact rounding at both levels.

items.title: Causal inference in staggered adoption panels: The correct comparison set depends on your intervention
items.summary: A powerful data structure for causal inference is staggered adoption: many units are observed over many time periods, during which some units adopt an irreversible treatment at various time points while others remain untreated. Popular methods that apply in this setting include difference in difference, fixed effects, matching, and synthetic control. All of these methods compare the future outcomes of treatment adopters and non-adopters to answer the question: for units who adopt treatment, what outcomes would have been realized if they had remained untreated? We show that this question actually hides two very different causal questions of interest. The first is what would have happened under a momentary intervention to prevent treatment at its factual adoption time. The second is what would have happened to a treated unit under a longitudinal ban preventing treatment at all periods until outcome measurement. We show how to answer each question under conditionally ignorable treatment adoption or under parallel trends. We highlight that common methods cannot answer the second question because this question requires a time-varying comparison set with time-varying weights.

items.title: Simulation in discrete choice models evaluation: SDCM, a simulation tool for performance evaluation of DCMs
items.summary: Discrete choice models are widely used in economics, transportation, and marketing to explain and predict how decision makers choose among a finite set of alternatives. The resulting choices depend on the socioeconomic characteristics of the decision makers, the attributes of the alternatives, and the conditions under which the decision is made. Because these factors interact in complex ways, and because real experiments raise confidentiality concerns, take time, and are costly, controlled experimentation with real respondents is often impractical. Simulation offers an alternative in which the data-generating process, and hence the true parameters, are known. This paper connects discrete choice modeling, experimental design, and simulation. We review the three areas in a common notation and state the results on which the simulation approach relies. We then formalize a simulation tool that combines an experimental design with a behavioral model of artificial agents to generate synthetic stated choice data, and we prove that the generated choices follow a panel mixed multinomial logit model with known parameters. On this basis we define measures of estimator performance and of the discrepancy between simulated and real data, illustrate the tool with a stated choice experiment on the willingness to pay for environmental attributes of roses, and discuss the behavioral factors that separate simulated choices from real ones.

items.title: A Resource Allocation Tournament
items.summary: We introduce and analyze a round-robin simultaneous resource allocation contest, motivated by sports leagues and other competitive environments where agents must distribute limited resources across multiple encounters. Players allocate resources in advance to matches against all opponents, and match outcomes are determined by relative allocations. We study two payoff schemes: total points, where players accumulate rewards for each win, and winner-takes-all, where only the tournament winner is rewarded. For three players, we provide complete equilibrium characterizations under both schemes. For four or more players, we show that the total points payoff admits Blotto-type equilibria, while the winner-takes-all payoff requires numerical and algorithmic analysis. To address this, we develop a best-response dynamics algorithm with stochastic inertia and use it to approximate equilibria in games with four and five players.

items.title: Prospect Theory in Large Language Models: A Meta-Analysis of Loss Aversion, Diminishing Sensitivity, and Probability Weighting
items.summary: Prospect theory splits risky choice into three parts: loss aversion, measured by the relative weight of losses to gains, $λ$ (e.g., $λ= 2$ implies that losses weigh twice as much as gains), diminishing sensitivity to the size of outcomes (i.e., the curvature and linearity of the value function), and the nonlinear weighting of probabilities. I examined whether Large Language Models (LLMs) display the same properties as people by meta-analyzing 102 fitted estimates from 11 studies covering 32 language models. The three components emerge differently. Loss aversion is modest: the pooled $λ$ is 1.26 (95% CI 1.06 to 1.46), far below the strongest human meta-analytic estimate ($λ= 1.96$) and compatible with more conservative ones (1.07 and 1.31). Matched by design, LLMs are compatible with people when gains and losses are symmetric ($λ= 1.15$ against 1.07), but well below them when losses are smaller than gains (1.46 against 2.3), where human loss aversion is strongest. Value functions are close to linear rather than concave under the Tversky-Kahneman method (1.01, against a human value of 0.67), but more concave than in people under the Tanaka method (0.52, against 0.67), so diminishing sensitivity depends on how it is measured. Probability weighting shows a human-like inverse S shape ($γ= 0.81$ under Tversky-Kahneman and 0.84 under the Tanaka method), though on few studies. In sum, LLMs show little loss aversion and little diminishing sensitivity, but retain human-like probability distortion, yet these generalizations shift when looking at specific model families and fitting methods.

items.title: The Capability Transfer: Cohort Reversal, Codified Expertise, and the Adaptability Tax of AI Transformation
items.summary: Most analyses of AI and employment ask which jobs are exposed. This paper asks what happens to the pipeline that produces experts. It extends the model of Caosun and Aral (2026) from a single worker to a firm with two cohorts, juniors and seniors, and studies how expertise formation changes when codified work is automated. Because junior work is the most codified, demand for juniors falls first; the stock of seniors falls later but further, as the pipeline stops replacing the experts who retire. In the baseline calibration, junior demand bottoms out about a fifth below its 2022 level before recovering most of that ground, while the senior stock falls by a quarter and later halves. Because expertise forms through unassisted practice on work that AI cannot do, the time needed to develop an expert from within rises from about five years to nine. The costs fall on a different party from the one that decides on adoption: a manager with a three-year horizon sets AI use to maximise near-term output, cutting the wage bill by 21 percent while the capacity of the firm on work AI cannot do falls by two-fifths and its output on that work goes unserved once the pipeline runs thin. Two key parameters are not yet measured, so the results are scenarios rather than forecasts. The paper proposes three indicators organisations can track: the unaided practice juniors get on work AI cannot do, senior time spent on such work, and the years it takes to develop an expert.

items.title: Unambiguous Efficiency of Random Allocations
items.summary: When allocating indivisible objects via lottery, planners often use ordinal mechanisms, which elicit agents' rankings of objects rather than their full preferences over lotteries. In such an ordinal informational environment, planners cannot differentiate between utility profiles that induce the same ranking of objects. We propose the criterion of unambiguous efficiency: regardless of how each agent extends their preferences over objects to lotteries, the allocation is Pareto efficient with respect to the extended preferences. We compare this with the predominant efficiency criterion used for ordinal mechanisms. As an application to mechanism design, we characterize all efficient and strategy-proof mechanisms satisfying certain regularity conditions.

items.title: Crowdsearch
items.summary: A common economic process is crowdsearch, wherein a group of agents is invited to search for a valuable object, such as a software vulnerability or a proof-of-work nonce. We study a binary model of crowdsearch in which agents with heterogeneous search costs decide whether or not to search. Inviting more agents directly expands the pool of potential searchers, but it also increases competition for the prize and lowers individual search incentives. This crowding-out effect may dominate, so that inviting more agents can lower the probability of finding the object. We show that inviting an unlimited crowd need not guarantee success. We also provide sufficient conditions, based on the lower-tail behavior of the cost distribution, under which the probability of success is eventually increasing or eventually decreasing in the number of agents.

items.title: The Anatomy of Dependence in Multivariate Ordered Choice
items.summary: When individuals make simultaneous decisions across multiple ordered dimensions, standard multivariate ordered choice models impose narrow bracketing, with each dimension decided as if the others did not exist. We develop a general rectangular structure model capturing broad bracketing while nesting the standard model. The framework introduces two layers of dependence, one through the threshold structure associated with decision rules and the other through the correlation of latent utilities. We provide microfoundations, prove identification, and discuss estimation. We showcase the model in applications to parental investment in children's education, cryptocurrency familiarity and expectations, and health insurance, where the latter separates moral hazard from adverse selection.

items.title: Identifying level-$k$ reasoning in repeated games: Strategies, beliefs, and cognitive ability
items.summary: In this paper, we identify level-$k$ reasoning in repeated games that operates at the level of a supergame strategy. First, we develop a model of level-$k$ reasoning that incorporates choices over strategies as well as beliefs about the strategies chosen by others. Then, jointly using elicited strategies and beliefs about strategies from the indefinitely repeated Prisoner's Dilemma, and applying a new notion of balance-optimal error tolerance, we classify a substantial fraction of subjects as level-1 or level-2. Moreover, we show that when level-$k$ reasoning operates at the level of a repeated-game strategy, cognitive ability and experience predict higher level reasoning.

items.title: Beyond city pairs: Higher-order information in urban growth across borders
items.summary: We apply higher-order information measures to urban growth across borders and spatial units. We analyse 8,808 functional urban areas using gridded GDP estimates allocated from national accounts. Negative estimated O-information occurs in 29.93% of cross-border triplets and 2.00% of domestic triplets. This fifteen-fold contrast falls to fourfold at comparable dependence strength and persists under data-quality restrictions. Target-specific decompositions show how information overlaps or combines across cities. Administrative subdivisions have mean O-information within matched random-map ranges inside countries. These findings show why interpreting geographic dependence requires specifying comparison cities and spatial units, while economic connections remain to be established independently.

items.title: Envy-free, efficient and strategy-proof division of a heterogeneous good between two agents
items.summary: We study the division of $[0,1]$ between two agents, each receiving a closed subinterval, under ordinal preferences that need not be additive. A monotonic preference has a unique balanced cut, at which the agent is indifferent between the left and the right piece. On a domain of monotonic preferences, a strategy-proof, envy-free and Pareto efficient rule exists if and only if the balanced cuts of the preferences in the domain take at most two distinct values; when they take exactly two, the divide-and-choose rules are the only such rules. For preferences single-peaked in quantity, which are additive only if monotonic, the three properties are compatible when the agents' most preferred bundles can be assigned simultaneously.

items.title: Testing for peer effects in short panels without identifying the network structure
items.summary: We propose an instrument-based test for peer effects in short-T panels when the underlying network is unknown. The test avoids estimating the network by aggregating pairwise comparisons between covariate-projected outcomes of potential peers and residualized own outcomes. The statistic is designed for fixed-T, large-N settings with individual fixed effects, heterogeneous slopes, heteroskedasticity, and serial dependence within units. We also develop a weighted extension that accounts for additive common time effects. The limiting distribution is standard Gaussian when the norm of the projected component of the outcomes is bounded away from zero, but can be nonstandard when it is local to zero. We derive a conditional Gaussian limit experiment and a feasible conditional Monte Carlo procedure to obtain uniformly valid critical values. Monte Carlo evidence shows that the conditional procedure leads to accurate size control while retaining power against latent peer-effect alternatives.

items.title: Voting with Partial Orders: The Plurality and Anti-Plurality Classes
items.summary: In the theory of voting, the Plurality rule for preferences that come in the form of linear orders selects the alternatives most frequently appearing in the first position of those orders, while the Anti-Plurality rule selects the alternatives least often occurring in the final position. We explore extensions of these rules to preferences that are partial orders, offering axiomatic characterisations for them.

items.title: The missing price feedback: Why studies overstate local grid peaks from synchronized home batteries under real-time pricing
items.summary: Existing studies consistently find that home batteries optimized against real-time electricity prices create new load peaks in local distribution grids. This is because all assets respond to the same price signal in sync. However, most of these studies treat wholesale prices as exogenous, i.e., unaffected by that very response. This paper argues that treating prices as non-responsive biases the result: in reality, charging in low-price hours raises the wholesale price, which dampens the incentive to charge. In equilibrium, charging is spread out across hours. I test this by simulating households with rooftop solar and home batteries under a spot-based retail tariff, using a model of equilibrium wholesale prices calibrated to German data for 2025. With exogenous prices, my results confirm the finding from the previous literature: synchronous charging pushes the coincident import peak of the local grid to 83% above its no-battery level. With endogenous prices, the same fleet leaves the peak 6% below the no-battery benchmark. In other words, treating prices as endogenous reduces the coincident peak at high battery penetration nearly by half. This finding is robust across alternative price functions and exogenous price paths, different measures of the coincident peak, 20 scenario variations, and three historical years. I conclude that while new local peaks remain possible, particularly in grids where battery deployment runs ahead of the national average, the risk and magnitude are considerably smaller than the existing literature suggests.

items.title: Risk Sensitivity and Stationary Equilibrium in Incomplete Markets
items.summary: We study stationary equilibrium and comparative statics in an incomplete market economy with risk-sensitive preferences. We prove that a stationary equilibrium exists for every nonnegative degree of risk sensitivity. With independent income, greater risk sensitivity weakly raises aggregate saving at fixed prices and weakly lowers the smallest and the largest equilibrium interest rates. With stochastically monotone Markov income, these comparisons hold when the lower risk-sensitivity parameter is sufficiently small or the upper parameter sufficiently large. For pairs of intermediate values, however, greater risk sensitivity can lower saving, contrary to an existing result in the literature, and can raise the smallest and largest equilibrium rates. An exact decomposition identifies the forces driving these reversals.

items.title: Two-Point Dependent Wild Bootstrap for Weakly Dependent Estimating Equations
items.summary: This paper develops a general two-point dependent wild bootstrap (DWB) for weakly dependent estimating equations. Its key feature is that the two-point marginal distribution and the latent serial dependence specification can be chosen separately. The construction combines a normalized two-point distribution with a stationary latent Gaussian process via a Gaussian copula transformation, includes dependent Rademacher and Mammen multipliers, and nests the classical iid two-point wild bootstrap as the serially independent case. The induced multiplier autocovariances determine the lag weights in a corresponding heteroskedasticity- and autocorrelation-consistent (HAC) covariance estimator, which coincides exactly with the conditional covariance of the bootstrap estimating-equation sum. We establish first-order bootstrap validity for asymptotically linear estimators by showing that the matched-HAC estimator consistently estimates the long-run covariance and that the bootstrap estimating-equation sum converges conditionally to the same Gaussian limit as its original-sample counterpart, yielding valid HAC-studentized $z$-tests and the corresponding Wald and Lagrange multiplier tests. Monte Carlo experiments in nonlinear generalized method of moments (GMM) and linear regression, with common HAC studentization and matched multiplier covariances, show that dependent Rademacher generally yields better size control than Mammen and Gaussian DWB, especially for restricted $z$-tests. An application illustrates differences between asymptotic and bootstrap inference.

items.title: The Reaction of Financial Markets to the Releases of DeepSeek R1 and Kimi K3: A Critical Analysis
items.summary: This paper compares financial-market reactions to the releases of DeepSeek R1 in January 2025 and Kimi K3 in July 2026. Both AI models were presented as credible Chinese competitors near the capability frontier, but their releases conveyed different economic information. DeepSeek R1 combined open weights with unusually low reported training and inference costs, prompting investors to reassess expected demand for computing infrastructure and producing large stock-price decreases among semiconductor and data-centre-related firms. Kimi K3 instead entered at broadly frontier prices and generated a market reaction concentrated more heavily among rival Chinese AI laboratories. Drawing on descriptive event-window evidence, model capability and cost comparisons, subsequent industry developments, and the historical diffusion of open-source software, the paper argues that open-weight models redistribute rents across the AI value chain rather than eliminating them. Incumbents remain protected by complementary assets including distribution, product bundling, switching costs, proprietary data, serving capacity, and contractual trust. The analysis suggests that investors and policy makers should assess risks looking not only at model capability, but also at the ownership and durability of complementary assets across the AI value chain.

items.title: Joules-to-GDP: How Much Economic Value Do AI Systems Produce per Unit of Energy?
items.summary: An AI system can produce more economically valuable work while delivering less value for the energy it consumes. We therefore ask: How much economic value does an AI system create per unit of energy consumed? We formalize economic value in two ways: (1) net dollar value, the output's dollar value minus AI-system execution cost, and (2) time saving, the expert's completion time minus the AI system's completion time. Dividing each by measured end-to-end energy yields Net Value per Joule (NVJ) and Time Saving per Joule (TSJ), reported in USD/MJ and hours/MJ. We study 220 public GDPval tasks across 44 occupations, serving five open-weight models locally and evaluating four accelerator types. First, the occupation groups where AI systems succeed most often, deliver the greatest dollar value, or save the most time do not necessarily provide the greatest economic return per joule. For example, among the tested tasks, engineering work delivers about 10% more net dollar value per task than software development. Yet software development delivers about 27% more net value per joule. Second, GLM 5.2 delivers the highest average net dollar value, at $72.27 per task using 0.430 MJ, equivalent in energy to about four hours of active laptop use. By contrast, Gemma 4 31B delivers 56% of that net dollar value using just 23% of the energy, achieving approximately 2.5 times the NVJ and 2.8 times the TSJ. Third, across four single-accelerator deployments, Qwen3.6-27B's NVJ varies by a factor of 4.32 and TSJ by 9.27, with B200 leading both. Additionally, one and eight H100s deliver similar net dollar value, but eight reduce completion time by 22% at 3.24 times the energy. Our framework makes output value and expert time saving under an energy budget explicit objectives for improving models, accelerators, and software, while offering a new basis for assessing AI's potential economic effect on occupational work.

items.title: A Weakly Group Strategy-Proof and Pareto-Stable Matching Mechanism with Two-Sided Indifferences under Gross Substitutes
items.summary: We study finite many-to-one matching markets with indifferences on both sides and publicly known firm preferences over sets of workers. A standard approach breaks ties uniformly at random and runs deferred acceptance, which is strategy-proof for workers but may select a weakly stable matching that is Pareto dominated under the agents' original preferences. For the broad class of markets in which each firm's preferences admit a gross substitutes (GS) representation, we construct a deterministic generalized deferred acceptance mechanism that is weakly stable, Pareto efficient with respect to both sides, worker weakly group strategy-proof, and implementable in strongly polynomial time given value oracles for the GS representations. This domain includes nonresponsive firm preferences, such as additive scores under matroid constraints and assignment values. Our analysis bridges ordinal matching with indifferences and competitive equilibria under imperfectly transferable utility. Although the mechanism uses only ordinal comparisons, it returns a seller-optimal equilibrium matching of a tiered auxiliary market, and the equilibrium structure of this market yields the stability, efficiency, and incentive guarantees.

items.title: Identification and Estimation in Panel Data Models with Nonparametric Two-Way Fixed Effects
items.summary: We study identification and estimation of panel data models that are characterised by a common, potentially, infinite-dimensional parameter, $θ$ and an unknown transformation $g(α_{i},γ_{t})$ of two-way fixed effects $(α_{i},γ_{t})$ that are themselves unknown. We treat $g$ as a nonparametric object to be identified/estimated together with $θ$ and $(α_{i},γ_{t})$. We first provide high-level assumptions under which $θ$ together with the image of $g$, $\{g(α_{i},γ_{t})\}$, is identified. Next, we show that, under weak regularity conditons on $g$ and the underlying distribution of $(α_{i},γ_{t})$, this image in turn allows us to separately identify normalised versions of g and the fixed effects. This is achieved by using a finite number of leading singular functions of $g$ as proxies (normalised versions) of the fixed effects. Our identification argument is constructive in the sense that it leads to natural estimators of the parameters of interest.

items.title: The Delegation Divide: An Open Index of AI-Agent Delegability across Occupations and Countries
items.summary: 35.2% of task time in world employment is at least partly delegable to AI agents in 2026, and only 2.5% can be handed over in full. Existing measures score exposure to generative AI, mostly for the United States. We build the Agent Delegability Index (ADI): two language models rate all 18,796 O*NET 30.2 task statements on a frozen, preregistered rubric of delegation levels and barriers; tasks are mapped to 433 ISCO-08 unit groups and weighted by ILOSTAT employment in 146 countries. Four findings. First, delegable employment rises with income, from 22.5% in low-income to 48.7% in high-income countries, a slope of 7.23 percentage points per log point of GDP per capita. This delegation divide is compositional: the physical barrier dominates the jobs poorer countries employ most. Second, at the occupation level ADI tracks exposure closely (r = 0.93 with Eloundou et al. and 0.89 with Felten et al.), above the preregistered bound of 0.80; ADI adds delegation levels and barriers on top of exposure, for the world, not a new ranking of occupations. Third, full delegation is rare and peaks for tasks that take a human about twelve minutes (11.8 minutes). Fourth, the preregistered adoption gap is not supported: across 101 countries, delegability and observed AI usage correlate at r = 0.86, and the gap between them is not wider in middle-income countries (p = 0.27). Model agreement is kappa = 0.77; a blind human rating of 300 tasks agrees with the model consensus at kappa = 0.85, and an agentic panel with web search at kappa = 0.87. We release the index, the atlas, the prompts and an MCP server at https://github.com/Cespial/delegation-divide.

items.title: Selling to Non-linear Agents: A Demand-Based Auction
items.summary: Auctions allocate scarce goods, from car licenses to online advertising, to buyers whose utilities are often not linear in money, as with budgets or risk aversion. We ask how a seller should sell to such buyers and what learning their preferences is worth. We propose demand-based auctions, which elicit demand curves and are dominant-strategy incentive compatible for any non-linear utilities. The revenue-maximizing one takes familiar second-price forms and is max-min optimal when the seller observes only demand curves. Under standard assumptions, learning risk attitudes beyond demand curves adds relatively little revenue, as does learning budgets unless they correlate with values.

items.title: Equilibrium Architecture in Multi-Battle Contests with Count-Dependent Prizes
items.summary: We study how aggregating local victories shapes participation and equilibrium uniqueness. Two contestants with possibly different marginal costs compete across identical Tullock battlefields with discriminatory power at most one. A nonconstant, nondecreasing, symmetric schedule divides a fixed prize by victory count. We establish existence and show that every realized equilibrium allocation divides effort equally across battlefields. Equilibrium is unique through six battlefields, with at most two effort levels per contestant; seven first permits multiple equilibria or randomization by both contestants. The prize schedule and technology, not the cost ratio, determine whether equilibria use infinitely many effort levels; in that case, cost asymmetry changes only the higher-cost contestant's participation probability. Under majority rule, we characterize the unique equilibrium for every battlefield count and cost ratio.

items.title: Selling Evidence Bit by Bit
items.summary: We study the sale of an asset to competitive buyers. Before the sale, the seller can buy hard information about the asset from an intermediary who designs and prices a test to maximize his revenue guarantee across equilibria. The test consists of one or more signals, and the seller privately chooses which subset of signals to buy and selectively discloses their realization to the buyers. We show that the intermediary benefits from splitting information into multiple signals and characterize his maximal revenue guarantee as the cumulative entropy of the asset value distribution. This guarantee is achieved by a sequence of ``skim from the top'' tests with binary, i.i.d.\ signals and additive pricing. Furthermore, any sequence of tests that achieves the maximal guarantee reveals the asset's value in the limit. For binary values, we also characterize the revenue guarantee for any given number of signals, and show that it is achieved by a test that corresponds to a ``Swiss cheese" model of failure with conclusive good news.

items.title: Measuring Geopolitical Alignment and Economic Growth
items.summary: We introduce an event-based measure of bilateral geopolitical alignment from 373,020 events across 193 countries over 1960-2024, compiled using large language models and validated with external benchmarks and a human audit. Aggregating alignment with major nations summarizes each country's external geopolitical environment. In local projections using within-country variation, a sustained one-standard-deviation improvement in this environment is followed by about 10 percent higher GDP per capita after 25 years. This relationship is similar across major-nation partners and historical periods, and is accompanied by greater stability, investment, trade openness, and productivity. Accounting exercises map observed realignments into substantial GDP differences.

items.title: Randomized Recruitment Driven Sampling
items.summary: Surveys are critical inputs for research and policy, yet, enumerating a sampling frame is logistically infeasible or financially nonviable in many circumstances, such as during pandemics, natural disasters, or armed conflict. Respondent Driven Sampling (RDS) does not require a sampling frame, yet non-random peer recruitment often introduces substantial bias, particularly under high homophily. We introduce and evaluate Randomized Recruitment Driven Sampling (RRDS), a cellphone-based adaptation of RDS that incorporates researcher-controlled randomization into each recruitment wave. While standard RDS is necessary for stigmatized groups where network transparency is infeasible, RRDS is designed for low-stigma populations that become difficult to access due to logistical barriers. In these contexts, RRDS enforces the random recruitment assumption that traditional RDS relies upon but rarely achieves. Through simulation and an experiment surveying Bangladeshi garment workers during the COVID-19 pandemic, we demonstrate that RRDS produces less biased estimates and improved confidence interval coverage compared to traditional RDS. RRDS offers a scalable, remote-compatible alternative for studying low-stigma groups in challenging contexts where large-scale probability sampling is unsafe or infeasible.

items.title: Austerity, Gender, and Multidimensional Deprivation Among Older Europeans: Evidence from SHARE
items.summary: This paper studies whether fiscal consolidation is associated with deeper multidimensional deprivation among older women than among older men, and through which channel. Using six waves of SHARE across eleven European countries, it builds a multidimensional deprivation index spanning functional health, economic insecurity, and social exclusion, and relates it to the cyclically adjusted primary balance (CAPB) at the country-wave level in a two-way fixed-effects model. Consolidation raises deprivation on average with a null average gender gap, which is later found to conceal regional heterogeneity where the gender gap is positive and significant in Southern and Eastern Europe, and absent in Continental/Nordic Europe. This regional pattern holds under individual clustering but does not survive clustering at the country level. Further, the economic insecurity channel the literature would predict runs in the opposite direction, with men's measured insecurity rising more steeply than women's; this is the only dimension whose interaction survives country-level inference. Social exclusion exhibits a larger gender effect, concentrated in the Eastern and Southern Europe, but it is significant only under individual clustering. The gendered cost of austerity among older Europeans is therefore neither uniform across welfare regimes nor routed through income, though the evidence for its social channel is inconclusive.

items.title: Identification of Latent Group Effects under Conditional Calibration
items.summary: We study identification of a structural group effect when the group indicator $G\in\{0,1\}$ is unobserved but the analyst observes a calibrated probability score $p$ satisfying $E[G\mid p,X]=p$. Under a constant-coefficient structural mean model, the latent-group coefficient $τ$ is point-identified by a closed-form ratio of observable moments whose denominator is the residual score variance $V^{*}=E[(p-E[p\mid X])^2]$. Identification fails exactly when the score is a deterministic function of $X$; we construct an explicit continuum of observationally equivalent models showing the failure is genuine. The marginal latent mean gap decomposes as $τ$ plus a compositional term that is itself identified in closed form, and we characterise when the two coincide. The oracle estimator is $\sqrt{n}$-consistent and asymptotically normal with a closed-form sandwich variance. Under calibration error bounded by $δ$, the bias obeys a sharp bound proportional to $δ/V^{*}$, and hard-threshold classification attenuates the estimated gap. Monte Carlo experiments confirm the theory, including the variance-weighted estimand under heterogeneous effects.

items.title: Monetary Policy Forecast Errors and Inflation Compensation under Sovereign Stress in Brazil
items.summary: This paper examines whether inflation compensation around Brazilian monetary policy decisions is associated differently with policy forecast errors when sovereign spreads are relatively elevated. Public Tesouro Direto quotations, meeting-specific Focus forecasts and a lagged EMBI indicator yield 68 three-year and 60 five-year event observations. The outcome is a matched-horizon retail yield proxy; the policy variable is the announced Selic target minus a preceding-week survey mean. At three years, a 10-basis-point forecast error is associated with 4.14 basis points less compensation repricing in the high-spread state than in the low-spread state, but the restricted wild cluster test gives a two-sided p-value of 0.1018. The estimated total high-state response is -0.42 basis points, with a pointwise 95 percent interval of [-2.25, 1.41]. The five-year interaction is sensitive to pandemic meetings and changes sign when 2020 is excluded. A common sample of 43 events does not establish a maturity gradient. A supplementary comparison on extended windows is also sensitive to the policy measure. The evidence is therefore inconclusive about state dependence. Survey timing, sparse maturity support and daily retail quotations prevent these associations from identifying a structural monetary shock, a pure inflation-risk premium or fiscal dominance.

items.title: Causal Inference under Dynamic Selection and Latent Heterogeneity
items.summary: I study dynamic treatment effects in panel data under staggered adoption when treatment timing depends jointly on unobserved time-invariant heterogeneity and time-varying pretreatment covariates, including lagged outcomes. Untreated potential outcomes follow a nonparametric dynamic panel model that allows flexible interactions between time-varying covariates and latent heterogeneity. I use pretreatment outcome histories to find individuals with similar time-invariant latent factors, and the key requirement is that these histories are sufficiently informative about those latent factors. I develop an identification strategy for the dynamic average treatment effect on the treated (ATT) and propose kernel-based doubly robust estimators for the dynamic ATT. I further combine double cross-fitting with undersmoothing and show that, under suitable regularity conditions, the proposed estimators are root-n consistent, asymptotically normal, and asymptotically unbiased. The simulation study demonstrates that the proposed method provides accurate inference across a wide range of data-generating processes. I illustrate the method with an application to the U.S. family planning program studied by Bailey (2012) and reestimate its effect on fertility rates.

items.title: Limits of Disclosure in Search Markets
items.summary: This paper examines competitive information disclosure in search markets with a mix of savvy consumers, who search costlessly, and inexperienced consumers, who face positive search costs. Savvy consumers incentivize truthful disclosure; inexperienced consumers, concealment. With both types, equilibrium features partial disclosure, which persists despite intense competition: in large markets, firms always conceal low valuations. Inexperienced consumers may search actively, but only in small markets. While savvy consumers benefit from increased competition, inexperienced consumers may be harmed. Changes in search costs have non-monotone effects: when costs are low, sufficient reductions increase informativeness and welfare; when costs are high, the opposite.

items.title: The Limits of Price Discrimination When the Market Is Unknown
items.summary: Bergemann, Brooks, and Morris (2015) characterize the consumer and producer surplus pairs that segmentation can produce when the distribution of values is known. I fix only the set of possible values and characterize the pairs that some market and some segmentation can produce. They form a convex polygon. Its outer edge is the largest efficient surplus a market can have when its uniform-price profit is capped, net of that profit, and truncated equal-revenue markets attain it. At the values no segmentation is needed; strictly between two values, reaching the frontier requires splitting a market into two extremal markets. With a continuum of values up to $\bar{v}$, consumer surplus is at most $π\ln(\bar{v}/π)$ when producer surplus (the seller's profit) is $π$, this bound is reached without segmentation, and no market gives consumers more than $\bar{v}/e$.

items.title: Paying for Information, Not for Clicks: A Block-Level Publisher Content Marketplace for AI Answers
items.summary: We propose a publisher content marketplace that allocates payments for information used in AI-generated answers. The unit of attribution is a ``lego block:'' a distinct fact or piece of commentary that may appear in articles from multiple publishers. A simple news-reading model connects three payment rules: equal sharing among all publishers reporting on a block, rewarding the publisher who reported a block first, and rewarding indispensable contributions. Each can be represented within a Shapley-value framework. We evaluate the framework using answers to 1,974 search-engine queries about a heavily covered news episode. When attribution considers only the articles retrieved for an individual query, most cited blocks appear unique, and the rules produce nearly identical allocations. A global index covering the full news corpus reveals overlap across publishers, making the choice of payment rule consequential. Premium publishers, defined as established outlets with substantial newsgathering operations, receive 42% of allocated value under equal sharing, compared with 46-50% under a first-publication rule, depending on the treatment of publication timestamps. These findings highlight the importance of a shared global index that records which publishers provide each block and when they published it. Attribution restricted to the sources retrieved for an individual answer lacks the information needed to distinguish these payment policies.

items.title: Policy Learning with Observational Data: The Case of Hepatitis C Treatment for HIV/HCV Co-Infected Patients
items.summary: Decision-makers frequently must choose a single action from a finite set of alternatives -- for example, physicians selecting a treatment, investors choosing a portfolio risk level, or judges determining sentences. To improve outcomes, policymakers often issue policy rules or guidelines to inform such choices. In this paper, I show how to generally derive policy rules from observational data in a multi-action framework under relatively weak assumptions about the underlying structure of the heterogeneous sampled population. Conditional average treatment effects (CATEs) are consistently estimated via a weighted K-means algorithm, assuming the outcome model is correctly specified within each homogeneous subgroup. I then use standard decision trees to implement feasible policy rules, allowing for both perfect and imperfect adherence to treatment. The methodology is applied to treatment options for Hepatitis C (HCV) among patients co-infected with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), a setting in which no uniform guideline exists for modern pharmaceutical therapies. The results identify a subgroup of patients with approximately an 80% probability of spontaneous HCV clearance without treatment. Estimation results also show that reallocating treatments among treated patients could have reduced total treatment costs by CAN$2.5-4.5 million while increasing aggregate health benefits relative to the status quo. These findings demonstrate that the proposed approach can generate improved, data-driven treatment guidelines for the management of HIV/HCV co-infected patients.

items.title: Moral Hazard in Delegated Bayesian Persuasion
items.summary: We study delegated Bayesian persuasion: a principal incentivizes an intermediary to design information via outcome-contingent transfers, while the intermediary privately chooses the experiment subject to convex costs. We characterize first-best implementability through a pair of alignment conditions on the principal's and intermediary's payoff indices. A local condition on the support of the target experiment is necessary; a global affine alignment condition is sufficient. We show that the gap between them is non-empty and provide a partial characterization of the intermediate region. When the first-best is unattainable, the principal's problem admits a virtual Bayesian persuasion representation: the second-best experiment maximizes the same concavified objective as the first-best, with the principal's payoff index distorted by a single scalar shadow price that summarizes the entire agency friction. Under entropy costs, moral hazard compresses posterior dispersion whenever the intermediary's utility differs across the actions it recommends. Explicit closed-form solutions for posteriors, mixing weights, and the optimal transfer schedule are derived for binary environments.

items.title: The Customer Is the Builder: How AI Coding Agents Are Rewriting the Economics of Software
items.summary: AI coding agents could change whether organizations buy software or build the functionality they need. We focus on organizations and professional buyers whose domain knowledge can help them specify and evaluate tools for their work. We define the software substitution frontier as the functions customers could build and maintain at an acceptable standard for less than buying them. Using public data, we compare growing capacity to build with indicators of market change. Since 2023, the length of benchmark tasks that leading agents can complete at 50 percent success, measured in human working time, has doubled about every 129 days. A broad search identified 575 potential open-source alternatives to selected commercial products, although some functional matches still require independent validation. The Craft suite produced 12 application repositories over 12.0 days of public development, but these remain early versions with unverified completeness and reliability. Market evidence is mixed: purchased software gained US investment share and tracked commercial installations grew. Yet 32 percent of respondents to an organizational survey reported forgoing at least one software purchase because their organization could build the functionality with coding agents. These self-reports do not establish the spending displaced or the reliability of the resulting tools. The gap motivates a warning: customers' capacity to build could affect individual buying decisions before a broad purchasing shift becomes visible. We examine this possibility using benchmark projections and observable market tests. The projections are an extrapolation, not a forecast of customer switching.

items.title: Certified Decisions
items.summary: Hypothesis tests and confidence sets are ubiquitous in empirical research, yet their connection to subsequent decision-making is often unclear. We view statistical inference as pairing recommended decisions with guarantees of their quality---or certificates---and develop a theory of certified decisions. Specifically, we attach P-certificates---upper bounds on loss that hold with probability at least $1-α$---to recommended actions. We prove that it is without loss to limit attention to P-certificates generated by minimax decisions over confidence sets, or what Manski (2021) terms "as-if decisions with a set estimate." We further show that such certificates allow safe adoption decisions for ambiguity-averse downstream decision-makers. A parallel argument applies to E-certified decisions obtained from e-values in settings with unbounded loss. We illustrate this view of statistical inference through an application to economic mobility and one to AI model routing.

items.title: Best Feasible Conditional Critical Values for a More Powerful Subvector Anderson-Rubin Test
items.summary: For subvector inference in the linear instrumental variables model under homoskedasticity but allowing for weak instruments, Guggenberger, Kleibergen and Mavroeidis (2019) (GKM) propose a conditional subvector Anderson and Rubin (1949) (AR) test that uses data-dependent critical values that adapt to the strength of the parameters not under test. This test has correct size and strictly higher power than the test that uses standard asymptotic chi-square critical values. The subvector AR test is the minimum eigenvalue of a data-dependent matrix. The GKM critical value function conditions on the largest eigenvalue of this matrix. Instead, this paper considers a data-dependent critical value function that conditions on the second-smallest eigenvalue, as this eigenvalue is the appropriate indicator of weak identification. We find that the data-dependent critical value function of GKM also applies to this conditioning and show that this test has correct size and power strictly higher than the GKM test when the number of parameters not under test is larger than one. This is the best feasible test, where we consider feasible to be within the class of conditioning on a single eigenvalue. Our proposed procedure further applies to the subvector AR test statistic that is robust to an approximate Kronecker product structure of conditional heteroskedasticity as proposed by Guggenberger, Kleibergen and Mavroeidis (2024), carrying over its power advantage to this setting as well.

items.title: Bias-Aware Inference in Regularized Regression Models
items.summary: We consider inference on a scalar regression coefficient under a constraint on the magnitude of the control coefficients. A class of estimators based on a regularized propensity score regression is shown to exactly solve a tradeoff between worst-case bias and variance. We derive confidence intervals (CIs) based on these estimators that are bias-aware: they account for the possible bias of the estimator. Under homoskedastic Gaussian errors, these estimators and CIs are near-optimal in finite samples for mean squared error and CI length. We also provide conditions for asymptotic validity of the CIs with an unknown and possibly heteroskedastic error distribution, and derive novel optimal rates of convergence under high-dimensional asymptotics that allow the number of regressors to increase more quickly than the number of observations. Extensive simulations and two empirical applications illustrate the performance of our methods.

items.title: Double machine learning for causal inference in a multivariate sample selection model
items.summary: We propose double machine learning (DML) estimators of the average treatment effect (ATE) and the average treatment effect on the treated (ATT) in the multivariate sample selection model with multiple ordinal selection equations. We establish asymptotic normality of the proposed estimators and study finite sample properties on simulated data. Specifically, the results of the analysis suggest that without addressing multivariate sample selection, the estimates of the causal parameters may be highly biased. However, the proposed estimators allow us to avoid these biases. Moreover, we apply the estimators to study the effect of female education on the log-wage ratio of spouses.

items.title: Semiparametric Dynamic Logit Model with Endogenous Networks
items.summary: This paper studies the identification and estimation of a semiparametric dynamic logit model with nonparametric link formation, in which a time-varying index of unobserved characteristics affects outcomes and links. The outcome depends on covariates, the past outcome, a fixed effect, and an unknown function of that index. Conditioning on a switch by the same agent across waves removes the fixed effect but not the change in the unknown function. When this change is common within network types and followed by a stable period, comparing two agents of the same network type, meaning they have the same probability of linking with each of the other agents, removes it and identifies covariate effects and state dependence. The pairwise conditional likelihood estimator is consistent, including when the index is continuous, and asymptotically normal when the index takes finitely many values and matches are exact. In simulations, bias falls with sample size, and coverage is near nominal among successful fits. The fixed-effects dynamic logit and pooled logits with peer-average controls remain biased when the index moves. A second estimator, conditioning on recovered network classes, is more precise. A feasibility exercise on the Glasgow Teenage Friends and Lifestyle Study examines how past use and pocket money affect adolescents' recorded tobacco or cannabis use and documents the data requirements.

items.title: Playing Against the Machine: Cooperation, Communication, and Strategy Heterogeneity in Repeated Prisoner's Dilemma
items.summary: We study whether communication sustains cooperation when the partner is an artificial intelligence. In a laboratory experiment (n = 234), human participants play indefinitely repeated Prisoner's Dilemma games against an AI chatbot (GPT-5.2) under one of three conditions: no communication, free-form chat before the first round of each supergame, or free-form chat before every round. A fourth treatment replaces the AI with another participant under the every-round protocol. Communication is the main determinant of cooperation with the AI, and a single exchange is enough: pre-play chat raises cooperation from 49% to 84%, while chatting before every round adds less than one percentage point, in contrast to the timing effect found between humans. Once communication is available, cooperation with the AI is no lower than with a human partner, so we find no evidence of the 'machine penalty' documented in the psychology literature. The partner's identity nonetheless shifts strategies: under identical communication, participants tend to reciprocate against a human but to cooperate unconditionally against the AI. Participants also keep their promises to cooperate while carrying out their threats to punish only about half the time. The AI opens cooperatively and rarely defects first, so these differences originate on the human side.

items.title: Memory Manipulation
items.summary: We study persuasion that works through memory: a manipulator alters the probabilities with which a Bayesian decision-maker recalls the signals he has received. The decision-maker corrects for the elevated or reduced probabilities of recalling different signals, and this correction disciplines what manipulation can achieve. Manipulation cannot move the average posterior. It backfires on decision-makers with few memories, whose sparse recall is evidence against the favored state, yet it is effective on those with many, who can be led to arbitrarily confident beliefs in the wrong state. It thickens the right tail of the belief distribution and, under Poisson memory, lowers its hazard rate. In a monopoly pricing application, the seller manipulates memory retrieval at high prices, and manipulation in turn raises the optimal price. In a narrative persuasion application, memory manipulation reduces information provision and creates echo chambers.

items.title: Learning in a Small/Big World
items.summary: Complexity and limited ability affect how we learn and make decisions under uncertainty. Using finite automata to model belief formation, this paper studies the characteristics of optimal learning behavior in small and big worlds, where the complexity of the environment is low and high, respectively, relative to the cognitive ability of the decision maker. The optimal long-run average payoff and distribution of actions are well approximated by the Bayesian benchmark in very small worlds, but the gap widens as the worlds get bigger. In big worlds, it can be optimal for the decision maker to ignore some states entirely, concentrating limited cognitive resources on a subset of states. This ``optimal ignorance'' is reminiscent of well-documented non-Bayesian learning patterns such as the use of heuristics, correlation neglect, and inattentive learning. The results establish a relationship between complexity, cognitive ability, and the scope for non-Bayesian learning behavior.

items.title: Demand Estimation for Rationally Inattentive Consumers
items.summary: We develop a rational-inattention BLP (RI-BLP) model for demand estimation from aggregate market shares, allowing for endogenous prices and unobserved preference heterogeneity. We establish conditions for uniqueness of market-share inversion and construct a simulated RI-BLP GMM estimator with instrumental-variable moments and market-share constraints. Under regularity and simulation-accuracy conditions, the estimator is consistent and asymptotically normal as the number of markets grows, with the number of products fixed. Monte Carlo experiments show accurate recovery of mean utility coefficients, with less precise estimates of dispersion parameters. In a canned-tuna application, RI-BLP and logit yield similar average own-price elasticities. Unlike logit, the fitted RI-BLP model implies that a price increase can reduce demand even for similar products and shift demand toward the outside option.

items.title: A measure of choice irrationality based on opposite judgements
items.summary: In many choice settings the decision maker (DM) adopts a criterion which is a mediation between her preference and its opposite. According to such compromise, the first i alternatives on top of the DM's taste are evaluated according to its negation. This pattern allows to define the compromise-based degree of irrationality, which quantifies the extent of the mediation embraced by the DM in her choice. Necessary and sufficient conditions characterizing this index are singled out. I investigate non rationalizable choices that display the lowest degree of irrationality, and I fully identify the preferences that explain the DM's picks by a minimal mediation between opposite judgments. These datasets account for some well known selection biases, such as second-best procedures, and the handicapped avoidance. I offer a simple characterization of the choice behavior that exhibits the most severe compromise, and I show that this subclass comprises almost all choices. Finally, some alternative measures of compromise are proposed, and compared with the score previously determined.

items.title: Estimating Nonseparable Selection Models: A Functional Contraction Approach
items.summary: We propose a novel method for estimating nonseparable selection models. We show that, for a given selection function and under suitable contraction conditions, the potential outcome distributions are nonparametrically identified from the selected outcome distributions and can be recovered using a simple iterative algorithm. This result enables a full-information approach to estimating selection models without imposing parametric or separability assumptions on the outcome equation. We propose a two-step estimation strategy for the potential outcome distributions and the parameters of the selection function and establish the consistency and asymptotic normality of the resulting estimators. Monte Carlo simulations demonstrate that our approach performs well in finite samples. The method is applicable to a wide range of empirical settings, including consumer demand models with only transaction prices, auctions with stochastic winning rules and incomplete bid data, and Roy-type models with data on accepted wages.

items.title: Climate-Driven Supply-Demand Matching Reshapes Global SolarEV Decarbonization Potential
items.summary: Rooftop photovoltaics (PV) can support rapid urban decarbonization, but their contribution is constrained by the imbalance between PV generation and demand, both shaped by local climate. Growing urban electric-vehicle (EV) deployment creates distributed storage near rooftop PV, shifting PV electricity across time. Here we simulate rooftop PV integrated with EVs as batteries across 5,000 grid cells globally, using hourly meteorology and climate-induced demand. We find that PV-EV systems can supply up to 84% of annual building and mobility electricity demand. Self-sufficiency is highest where daytime demand aligns with generation and seasonal variability remains limited.
